author: Suman Chakraborty
post_text:
Understanding #kubernetes pod lifecycle phases for effective #troubleshooting 🧐☸

✅ Pods follow a defined lifecycle, starting in the 'Pending' phase, moving through 'Running' if at least one of its primary containers starts OK, and then through either the 'Succeeded' or 'Failed' phases depending on whether any container in the Pod terminated in failure

✅ The phase of a #Pod is a simple, high-level summary of where the pod is in its lifecycle and it's part of "PodStatus" object that defines number of phases:
▶ 𝐏𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠: Pod has been accepted by the #k8s cluster, but one or more of the #containers has not been set up and made ready to run. This includes time a Pod spends waiting to be scheduled as well as the time spent downloading container images over the network
▶ 𝐑𝐮𝐧𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠:  Pod has been bound to a node, and all of the containers have been created. At least one container is still running, or is in the process of starting or restarting
▶ 𝐒𝐮𝐜𝐜𝐞𝐞𝐝𝐞𝐝: All containers in the Pod have terminated in success, and will not be restarted
▶ 𝐅𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐞𝐝: All containers in the Pod have terminated, and at least one container has terminated in failure. That is, the container either exited with non-zero status or was terminated by the system.
▶ 𝐔𝐧𝐤𝐧𝐨𝐰𝐧: the state of the Pod could not be obtained and it occurs due to an error in communicating with the node where the Pod should be running.

To track the phases between pod communication, "container lifecycle hooks" can be used to trigger events to run at certain points in a container's lifecycle !!

Ref: - https://lnkd.in/gsm8N64Q

author: Carl Collins Chwabo
post_text:
DevSecOps: Building security into every stage of software delivery.

Security can no longer be a final checkpoint before production. Waiting until the end of development leads to costly fixes, delayed releases, and avoidable vulnerabilities.

That is where DevSecOps comes in.
DevSecOps brings together Development, Security, and Operations teams to make security a shared responsibility across the software development lifecycle. The goal: deliver applications quickly while ensuring security controls are integrated, automated, and continuously improved.

Instead of asking “Has this been secured?” only before deployment, DevSecOps asks security-focused questions at every stage:

• Planning: What are the security requirements and risks?

• Development: Are developers following secure coding practices?

• Code review: Are secrets or vulnerable dependencies being introduced?

• CI/CD: Has the application passed automated security tests?

• Deployment: Is the cloud or container configuration secure?

• Production: Are logs monitored and vulnerabilities remediated quickly?
Key DevSecOps tools

• CI/CD: Jenkins, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI/CD

• SAST: SonarQube, Semgrep, Checkmarx

• SCA: Snyk, Dependabot, OWASP Dependency-Check

• Secrets detection: GitGuardian, Gitleaks

• DAST: OWASP ZAP, Burp Suite

• Container security: Trivy, Docker Scout

• IaC security: Checkov, tfsec

• Cloud security: Wiz, Microsoft Defender
for Cloud, AWS Security Hub

• Runtime monitoring: Splunk, Elastic Security, Wazuh, Falco

How to implement DevSecOps

1. Build a shared security culture across Dev, Sec, and Ops.

2. Define secure coding standards and threat-modeling practices.

3. Integrate automated security checks into CI/CD pipelines.

4. Apply risk-based security gates (block only on critical issues).

5. Secure cloud and container environments with least privilege and continuous scanning.

6. Monitor continuously in production and integrate incident response.

7. Measure improvement: time to remediate, vulnerabilities caught pre-prod, test coverage.

DevSecOps is about reducing risk without sacrificing innovation. When security is automated early and continuously, organizations can deliver faster, respond better, and build greater trust in their digital services.

For cybersecurity teams, developers, and IT leaders, the question is no longer whether security should be part of DevOps. The real question is: how early, how consistently, and how effectively are we integrating it?

author: Rust Jobs 🦀
post_text:
Rust Hiring Report – Q3 2026

Full report in the comments 👇

Over the past few years, we've worked closely with companies hiring Rust engineers and with developers looking for Rust roles. Both sides raise the same problem: there is little clear information about this market. This covers not just compensation, but where the jobs are, which industries are hiring, and how much of the work is remote.

A few months ago, we built a crawler (written in Rust) and an AI extraction pipeline. They find companies hiring Rust developers and evaluate their openings. Many job descriptions list several languages, such as "5+ years of experience in a backend language like Java, C++, Rust or Go". So a search for "Rust" can't tell you if the role actually uses Rust. Instead, we labelled a few hundred job descriptions by hand. Then we tuned an AI prompt until it got good at spotting real Rust positions.

Here are a few interesting points from the report:

- 753 open Rust job ads at 305 companies as of 16 Sep 2026.
- 2,898 ads mention Rust somewhere, but only 753 (26%) actually require it.
- 165 of the 305 companies have exactly one open Rust ad.
- Around 80% of ads want a senior or staff-level developer.
- US median advertised base: $205k for senior, $228.5k for staff/principal (base only, no equity or bonus).
- US pay data comes almost entirely from a few states with pay transparency laws. Elsewhere, disclosure is rare: only 25 of 165 European ads showed a range.
- Rust ads stay open slightly longer: 68% were still posted 45 days after they appeared, vs 56% for the average ad on the same boards over the same period.
- Defense/aerospace/space is the biggest sector by role count (22.7% of ads), but crypto/web3 has more companies hiring.
- Remote: 35% of ads that state a work setup are fully remote. Defense is the exception, at under 10%.
- Top employers by volume: Anduril (50 ads), Cloudflare (23), K2 Space (18), NVIDIA (13).

Limitations:

- We only count companies with a public, crawlable careers page. Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Apple and Meta are absent from every figure because we can't crawl their career sites, not because they don't hire for Rust.

- Salary data is rare outside the few US states that require employers to advertise it.

If you have ideas to improve the report or you spot errors, please let us know!

author: Simon Späti
post_text:
🔮 Navigating through the Trends of Data Engineering

Following up on my end-of-year #dataengineering predictions (https://lnkd.in/eD-dR8TJ), let's take a moment to reflect on the trends we saw in 2022 and what's brewing for 2023.

In #2022, we've seen a paradigm shift towards a declarative approach, shaping everything from infrastructure to orchestration and integration. The same principle lies at the heart of the flourishing semantic layer, promising an exciting, declarative future for metrics. ✨

Meanwhile, Rust is poised to revolutionize performance-heavy data applications, likely becoming the new Spark of the data world. For those navigating the small data seas, vector databases like DuckDB are becoming the go-to option, with an eye to support the AI wave on the horizon. Let's not forget - it's always about the data, not the other way around.

We've also noticed an upswing in metadata trends, with a focus on data cataloging, lineage, and discovery. And with GDPR and CCPA making waves, privacy and governance are becoming non-negotiables for every company, big or small.

Now, let's take a look at #2023. As we reveal the modern data stack (MDS), data modeling is making a comeback, offering a sense of order in the inevitable data chaos. But hold on, there's a caveat - many enterprises are grappling with how to harness the power of MDS. ️

This year is also witnessing the 'bundling' of MDS. Startups are consolidating (Transform into dbt), undergoing layoffs, and converging - evolution is the name of the game.

AI and generative AI, like our friend ChatGPT 🤖, are buzzing around, looking for ways to better integrate with data. While still more of a hype, many are keenly exploring these technologies' potential, and I can't wait to see how this story unfolds.

What changes have you noticed, and what predictions would you make for the future of data engineering? :)

post_text:
🚢 There might be thousands of pods running in our Kubernetes clusters but Are you using the “𝐑𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐝 𝐋𝐚𝐛𝐞𝐥𝐬 𝐛𝐲 𝐊𝐮𝐛𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐭𝐞𝐬” for labelling K8s resources? 🤔
✅ Here are the "Recommended Labels" which should be applied to every resource object:

1️⃣ 𝐚𝐩𝐩.𝐤𝐮𝐛𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐭𝐞𝐬.𝐢𝐨/𝐧𝐚𝐦𝐞
👉 The name of the application
👉 Example: “mysql”

2️⃣ 𝐚𝐩𝐩.𝐤𝐮𝐛𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐭𝐞𝐬.𝐢𝐨/𝐢𝐧𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞
👉 A unique name identifying the instance of an application. To assign a non-unique name, use "app.kubernetes.io/name"
👉 For example, WordPress has a "app.kubernetes.io/name" of "mysql" while it has an instance name, represented as "app.kubernetes.io/instance" with a value of "mysql-abcxzy".
👉 Every instance of an application must have a unique name.

3️⃣ 𝐚𝐩𝐩.𝐤𝐮𝐛𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐭𝐞𝐬.𝐢𝐨/𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧
👉 The current version of the application.
👉 Example: "5.7.21"
👉 Common forms of values include:
🔸 semantic version
🔸 the Git revision hash for the source code.

4️⃣ 𝐚𝐩𝐩.𝐤𝐮𝐛𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐭𝐞𝐬.𝐢𝐨/𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐨𝐧𝐞𝐧𝐭
👉 The component within the architecture.
👉 Example: “database”

5️⃣ 𝐚𝐩𝐩.𝐤𝐮𝐛𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐭𝐞𝐬.𝐢𝐨/𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐭-𝐨𝐟
👉 The name of a higher-level application this one is part of.
👉 Example: “wordpress”

6️⃣ 𝐚𝐩𝐩.𝐤𝐮𝐛𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐭𝐞𝐬.𝐢𝐨/𝐦𝐚𝐧𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐝-𝐛𝐲
👉 The tool being used to manage the operation of an application.
👉 Example: “helm”

✅ 𝐁𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐟𝐢𝐭𝐬 𝐨𝐟 𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐝 𝐥𝐚𝐛𝐞𝐥𝐬
👉 A common set of labels allows tools to work interoperably, describing objects in a common manner that all tools can understand.
👉 Easy to identify necessary information about any resource
👉 Helpful in creating standard templates, filters and selectors in a consistent way.

✍ If you are using any other labels which you consider important and should be part of all resources, let us know in the comments.

🔗 Kubernetes Docs: https://lnkd.in/gFKRuhbH

NVIDIA acaba de lanzar una plataforma para controlar a los agentes de IA que se salen de control.

OpenShell está construido principalmente con Rust.

author: Ali Turgut BOZKURT
post_text:
🐘 Her Şey İçin Ayrı Bir Teknoloji Şart mı? PostgreSQL ile Mimariyi Sadeleştirmek
Projeye başlarken hemen "Buraya bir Elasticsearch basalım", "Hemen bir Redis kuralım" demek çok cazip gelir. Ancak genç yazılımcıların en sık sorduğu sorulardan biri şudur: PostgreSQL tek başına bu ekosistemde nelere kadirdir, hangi durumlarda harici araçlara gerek kalmaz?
PostgreSQL'i doğru kullanarak hangi senaryolarda harici araçlar yerine sadece onu tercih edebileceğinizi 7 maddede derledim:
1. Full-Text Search (Arama Motoru Yerine)
Alternatif: Elasticsearch / Meilisearch
PostgreSQL Çözümü: pg_trgm ve tsvector özellikleri sayesinde, küçük ve orta ölçekli uygulamalarda harici bir arama motoru kurma maliyetine girmeden gelişmiş metin arama ve benzerlik sorguları yapabilirsiniz.
2. Şemasız Veriler (NoSQL / MongoDB Yerine)
Alternatif: MongoDB
PostgreSQL Çözümü: Güçlü JSONB veri tipi ve GIN indeksleri sayesinde, ilişkisel verilerle esnek JSON verilerini aynı masada harmanlayabilir; NoSQL esnekliğini SQL güvencesiyle birleştirebilirsiniz.
3. Hafifletilmiş İş Kuyrukları (Job Queue / RabbitMQ Yerine)
Alternatif: RabbitMQ / Kafka
PostgreSQL Çözümü: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED mekanizması ile kuyruk tabloları oluşturarak, ekstra bir message broker kurmadan güvenli ve transaksiyonel arka plan görev kuyrukları yönetebilirsiniz.
4. Zaman Serisi Verileri (Time-Series Yerine)
Alternatif: InfluxDB / Timescale (Harici)
PostgreSQL Çözümü: Açık kaynaklı TimescaleDB eklentisini ekleyerek, metrikleri, IoT verilerini ve zaman serisi analizlerini doğrudan PostgreSQL üzerinde yüksek performansla saklayabilirsiniz.
5. Operasyonel Sadırlık ve Tek Kaynak (Single Source of Truth)
Avantajı: Genç ekipler için birden fazla farklı veritabanını (Cache, Search, NoSQL, SQL) yönetmek, yedeklemek ve monitor etmek büyük bir operasyonel yükdür. PostgreSQL ile bu karmaşıklığı minimuma indirebilirsiniz.
6. Ne Zaman Sınır Aşılır? (Doğru Yeri Bilmek)
Sınır: Saniyede yüz binlerce cache okuması (Redis seviyesi) veya milyarlarca logun anlık aranması (Elasticsearch seviyesi) gerektiğinde PostgreSQL zorlanabilir. İhtiyacın boyutunu iyi analiz etmek gerekir.
7. Öğrenme Eğrisi ve Temelleri Sağlam Tutmak

w31b-agentic: 1.000 User, ca. 790 RPS, p99 81-150 ms, 0 Fails

peak-resilience: 300/500 User, ca. 1.300 RPS, p99 290-490 ms, checkout p99 400-640 ms, 0 Fails

Gerade der Commerce-Core ist spannend, weil dort die wirklich wichtigen Pfade liegen: Warenkorb, Checkout, Inventory, Orders, Payments.

Die API wurde explizit dafür gebaut, auch hohe Lastspitzen abzufangen. Diese Zahlen sind das Ergebnis von vielen kleinen Optimierungen an Hot Paths, Datenbankzugriffen, Transaktionen, Worker-Settings und den Lastprofilen selbst.

Was aber dabei wirklich wichtig ist:
0 Fehler. In jedem Profil.
Checkout ist als nächstes dran, was optimieren betrifft.

Performance entsteht nicht durch einen einzelnen Trick, sondern durch konsequentes Messen, Optimieren und wieder Messen.

Wichtig: Kein Redis/Kafka/Celery.

author: Mehmet Burçhan Gürses
post_text:
"Tablodan 10 milyon satır sildik ama veritabanı boyutu bir milimetre bile inmedi..." 🗄️👻
​PostgreSQL kullanan ekiplerin yaşadığı en sinsi performans krizlerinden biri: Disk dolmak üzeredir, eski kayıtları DELETE edersiniz; ancak disk kullanımı düşmediği gibi sorgular daha da yavaşlar.
​Sebebi PostgreSQL'in çok sürümlü eşzamanlılık kontrolü (MVCC) mimarisidir.
​PostgreSQL'de bir satırı sildiğinizde veya güncellediğinizde (UPDATE işlemi aslında bir DELETE + INSERTtir), kayıt diskten anında silinmez; sadece "ölü" işaretlenir: Dead Tuple.
​Bu ölü satırlar zamanında temizlenmezse:
​Tablo ve indeksler hayalet verilerle şişer (Table & Index Bloat),
​RAM ve disk I/O'su boş sayfaları taramakla tükenir,
​İndeks ağaçları gereksiz genişlediği için arama süreleri katlanır.
​PostgreSQL'i bu hayalet yükten kurtarmak için uyguladığım 3 kritik adım:
​🧹 Bloat ve Autovacuum Yönetiminde 3 Kural
​1️⃣ Varsayılan Autovacuum'a Güvenmemek:
PostgreSQL'in varsayılan autovacuum eşikleri büyük tablolarda çok geç devreye girer. Yoğun yazma alan tablolarda eşiği önden çekmek gerekir:
ALTER TABLE orders SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.05);
Böylece ölü satır oranı %5'e ulaştığı an temizlik başlar.
​2️⃣ İndeksleri Kilitlemeden Yenilemek (REINDEX CONCURRENTLY):
Veri silinse bile B-Tree indeks sayfaları işletim sistemine geri verilmez; indeks parçalanmış kalır. Canlı akışı ve yazmaları kesmeden indeksleri sıkılaştırmak için:
REINDEX TABLE CONCURRENTLY orders;
Bu komut çoğu zaman indeks boyutunu %60-70 küçültür ve belleği rahatlatır.
​3️⃣ Açık Kalan Transaction'ları (Idle in Transaction) Avlamak:
Arka planda unutulan tek bir açık transaction, kendisinden sonraki hiçbir ölü satırın VACUUM edilmesine izin vermez. idle_in_transaction_session_timeout ile bu asılı oturumları otomatik düşürmek şarttır.
​💼 Sizin de PostgreSQL altyapınızda şişen disk boyutları, anlamsızca yavaşlayan sorgular veya Autovacuum optimizasyonu ihtiyaçlarınız var mı?
​Veri tabanınızın depolama ve sorgu performansını zirveye taşımak için DM üzerinden bana ulaşabilirsiniz! 📥
​Sorgularınızın hafif, diskinizin ferah olduğu bir hafta dilerim! ☕

author: Amar Sharma
post_text:
The Story of PyTorch :
PyTorch, a leading deep learning framework, was created by Facebook's AI Research (FAIR) lab and launched in 2016 to offer a more flexible, Python-friendly approach for building neural networks.

Background

Before PyTorch, Facebook researchers used Torch, a deep learning framework built in Lua. However, Lua’s limited popularity made integration with Python projects difficult, so Facebook sought a Python-based alternative.

Key Innovations

FAIR’s goal was to build a framework that balanced easy experimentation with strong production support. A major feature was dynamic computation graphs, allowing models to adjust on-the-fly rather than relying on pre-set graphs—making experimentation faster and more adaptable.

Influences and Community

Inspired by the Japanese framework Chainer, PyTorch adopted dynamic graphs and a Pythonic design, which quickly made it a favorite among researchers. Being open-source, PyTorch attracted a large community of contributors, helping it become a strong rival to TensorFlow.

Growth and Industry Adoption

After PyTorch 1.0’s 2018 release, which improved stability and production features, adoption surged in research and industry alike. Facebook and Microsoft’s partnership also extended PyTorch’s presence on cloud platforms, such as Azure.

Today

PyTorch has become a go-to for tasks across fields like computer vision and natural language processing, valued for its flexibility, simplicity, and strong community support.

post_text:
Cursor is migrating from Solid.js to React, and from Tailwind to Stylex.

In a really interesting post from Lauren Tan (Principal Engineer at SpaceXAI / Cursor, ex-React core team), she explains why the move away from Solid:

- Main reasons were perf and maintainability. It was easier to create performance footguns in signal-based JS libraries as "reactivity causes a large amount of accidental fan out in large and complex apps".

- AI gets confused when writing React-like code in non-React libraries and quality of Solid.js code generated wasn't good, "everything ended up being accidentally tracked which caused so many perf problems". The React compiler solves most over-rendering perf problems.

Ultimately, the tech stack that makes the developer most productive will be preferred.

It'll be harder and harder for newer tech to gain adoption, especially for lower-level / foundation tech due to AI not being trained on them.

author: Jesus A. Palafox
post_text:
La noticia no es menor: OpenAI le retira el acceso a sus modelos a Cursor, el editor de código que se volvió inseparable del trabajo diario de cientos de miles de desarrolladores. El motivo, la adquisición de Cursor por parte de SpaceX, la empresa de Elon Musk.

Déjenme ser claro: esto no es una disputa técnica ni una decisión comercial rutinaria. Es la primera vez que vemos, a esta escala, cómo la geopolítica y las rencillas personales de los dueños de la infraestructura determinan quién puede usar qué modelo y bajo qué condiciones.

Cursor no es un cliente más. Es la puerta de entrada natural para que millones de programadores interactúen con modelos de frontera a diario. Que OpenAI decida cortar el grifo no es un capricho: es un recordatorio de que el acceso a la inteligencia artificial más capaz del mercado es un privilegio revocable, no un derecho adquirido.

Lo interesante del caso es que Cursor ya venía diversificando: usa modelos de Anthropic, Google y otros proveedores. Pero la lección queda sobre la mesa. Si mañana tu herramienta favorita depende de un modelo que su competidor controla, estás a una fusión de distancia de quedarte sin ella.

La pregunta incómoda es si esto empuja a más empresas a buscar soberanía tecnológica real, con modelos abiertos o propios, o si simplemente acelera la concentración del poder en unos pocos laboratorios que deciden quién juega y quién no.

Mientras tanto, los desarrolladores que construyen sobre estas plataformas harían bien en recordar que la nube de alguien más siempre será el castillo de alguien más. Y los castillos, en esta industria, cambian de dueño con frecuencia.

Già da agosto siamo a conoscenza dell’acquisizione di Cursor da parte di SpaceX per 60 miliardi di dollari. Una grande operazione finanziaria andata in porto con successo.

Se non fosse che a neanche un mese di distanza OpenAI ha annunciato che si avvarrà delle condizioni di recesso del contratto proprio a seguito del cambio di proprietario di Cursor. La decisione, che avrà effetti irreversibili dal 12 novembre, impedirà di fatto l’accesso nativo ai suoi modelli; ha inoltre specificato che il suo attuale modello di punta, Astra, non verrà reso disponibile su Cursor.

Le principali ragioni di questa scelta sono da ricercare sulle acredini precedenti verso Elon Musk che in più occasioni ha violato accordi. Ricordiamo l’ammissione di xAI di aver usato dati di OpenAI per addestrare Grok, oltre ad aver effettuato un blocco dati su X (ex Twitter) verso OpenAI. Insomma Sam Altman proprio non ne vuole sapere di collaborare con lui.
T
ra i due litiganti il terzo gode. Anthropic proprio non ci ha pensato un secondo a proporsi come "sostituto".
Praticamente sono corsi ad annunciare che aumenteranno la capacità di calcolo per supportare Claude 3.5 Sonnet all’interno di Cursor.

L’impatto delle scelte di OpenAI comunque non sembra eccessivamente tragico. Solo un 5% dei developer utilizzava GPT direttamente su Cursor e comunque anche dopo l’ultimatum del 12 novembre sembra che si potrà continuare ad usare la propria personale API Key, riducendo un po’ l’impatto delle scelte calate dall’alto.

Rimane comunque interessante analizzare questo specifico scenario perché la frattura tra i CEO di OpenAI e SpaceX potrebbe anche in futuro palesarsi magari in fronti opposti di eventuali tavoli per regolamentare l’AI.

Today at the TechEx Events show we were fortunate enough to have the opportunity to listen to several speakers and panelists, who shared their experiences Edge Computing. Where is the edge for you? For every person there may be a different definition for me it is the IoT device that is in a factory collecting data in near real time from the factory floor this could be a BLE, RFID , PLC, or other sensor or reporting mechanism that directly or indirectly impacts manufacturing, assembly processes that drive the Work in progress (WIP) with regards to production quality, compliance or velocity. For someone else it may be a smart phone, a drone generating data to the fist connection point for data backhaul or a storage point closest to the creation of data.

So, as you can see there are many definitions of the edge and there are just as many viewpoints to what edge compute really means, depending on your industry, if and what role you play in the IoT global ecosystem down to a local step by step process of data integration, collection and processing to include distribution to consumers who can be People, processes, or systems which benefit from the conditioned or raw data that is collected.

Especially interesting was the presentation on The Power of Differentiated 5G Networks: Enabling AR, AI, and APIs for the Emerging Immersive internet by Mischa Dohler the Vice President, Emerging Technologies @erickson #EdgeComputingExpo @IOTECHEXPO. During his presentation Mischa shared many informative related to 5G including 5G Networks, Devices and applications as they all apply to individual consumers and to Industry consumers about how there have been, notable shifts among consumers.

One analogy I found from Mischa's presentation today, is a key enabler and quite thought provoking was: You are on the 101 in San Jose you have a choice to make you can just keep traveling along at a slow pace in the traffic lanes with everyone else or you can move to the HOV lanes and move much faster. The takeaway is that it requires a decision and an investment to move much faster when traveling in heavy traffic or adopting changes due to technological advances.

This very informative presentation was followed by several other very good presentations including Scaling the Edge: Overcoming Challenges in Deployment and Integrations, Revolutionizing Customer Experiences with Edge Computing, and a presentation on the Hidden Networking Problems at the Edge by Jason Lovelace from IBM to round out day 1 of this excellent event.

author: Amol Kelkar
post_text:
We’ve all used classic UNIX command line utilities. For example, to count lines in a file:

> cat article.txt | wc -l
output: 46

Now, with Playbooks, you can create semantic, LLM-powered CLI utilities. For example:

> cat article.txt | summarize
output: The US penny, which cost nearly four cents to mint despite being worth one cent, was officially discontinued after 238 years of production. While the penny's removal from circulation is causing challenges for retailers and consumers - including rounding issues and potential legal complications in certain states - it will remain legal tender. The transition has been chaotic due to lack of government guidance, contrasting with how other countries like Canada and Australia handled similar currency phase-outs.

You can send a natural-language message to the utility to modify its behavior!

> cat article.txt | summarize --message "Use Pirate speak"
output: The penny, that scurvy dog of currency, has finally met Davy Jones' locker after 238 years o' sailin' the seven seas! The US Mint struck its final coin in June, and now merchants be facin' a tempest o' troubles—some be roundin' prices to the nearest nickel, while others be searchin' high and low fer pennies to keep their coffers balanced. Aye, 'tis a chaotic voyage ahead fer retailers and customers alike!

I use it to automate tasks like creating release notes by going through commit logs between two commits.
> release_notes --start v0.6.0 --end v0.7.0

This is same as
> playbooks run release_notes.pb --start v0.6.0 --end v0.7.0
output: See the release notes created with this utility at https://lnkd.in/gGjZrt8n

====

Here is another workflow: Search arXiv for today's papers on "AI agents", download the top 5 PDFs, convert each to markdown, extract future directions from each paper, then create a meta-summary as a bullet list of the most interesting research directions across all papers, and email the final synthesis to my@company.com with subject "Research proposals".

Do it in one line of bash script with semantic utilities search_arxiv and summarize --

search_arxiv --message "AI agents" | head -5 | xargs -I {}sh -c 'wget -qO- "{}" | pandoc -f pdf -t markdown | summarize --message "focus on future directions"'|\
summarize --message "Summarize as bullet list of most interesting research directions"|\
mail -s "Research proposals" my@company.com

====

What semantic command line utilities would you want?

author: DAVANTEL
post_text:
Cuándo tiene sentido la IA local: dispositivo, gateway o edge computer
"Edge AI" no describe un solo tipo de hardware. Elegir mal entre dispositivo IA dedicado, gateway edge o edge computer industrial es uno de los errores más caros en proyectos de analítica en tiempo real.
La decisión correcta depende de dos ejes independientes:
🔹 Intensidad de cómputo — ¿cuánto exige el workload?
🔹 Alcance de integración — ¿cuántos dispositivos, protocolos y funciones de red debe coordinar el hardware?
Dispositivo IA dedicado (ej. cámara con detección de objetos): ideal cuando una sola relación entrada-modelo-salida es estable. Fuerte en especialización, limitado en integración — no gestiona Modbus, múltiples PLCs ni backhaul celular.
Edge computing gateway: conecta equipos de campo, ejecuta aplicaciones locales y traslada datos seleccionados a sistemas superiores. Es la opción correcta cuando el resultado depende de combinar contexto — por ejemplo, vibración + corriente de motor + estado de PLC + entrada digital, para saber si una lectura elevada ocurrió en arranque o en producción normal.
Edge computer industrial: necesario solo cuando el proyecto exige varios streams de vídeo en alta resolución, modelos grandes, GPU o bases de datos pesadas — cargas que superan lo que una plataforma gateway-class puede ofrecer.
Un matiz importante: no todo gateway edge es un gateway de IA. El Robustel EG5100 es una plataforma sólida para bridging de protocolos y buffering, pero no incluye NPU dedicada. El EG5120 sí — añade CPU quad-core Cortex-A53 a 1.6GHz, hasta 4GB LPDDR4, 64GB eMMC y NPU de 2.3 TOPS, manteniendo routing celular, Ethernet Gigabit y gestión RCMS.
Y si el sitio necesita agregar más dispositivos (varias cámaras IP, más Ethernet, RS-422, HDMI, salidas de relé), el EG5200 ofrece la misma clase de CPU y NPU con 5 puertos Gigabit Ethernet frente a los 2 del EG5120 — la diferencia no es más potencia de IA, sino más alcance de integración.
📖 Artículo completo: https://nuel.ink/9eQ5B2

author: Nikolay Nikiforchuk
post_text:
Task Runners in n8n: The Upgrade We've Been Waiting For 🚀

I've been experimenting with n8n's new Task Runners, and I have to say—it changes how you extend and scale workflows. Until recently, extending n8n Code nodes with custom dependencies meant rebuilding the entire n8n Docker image every time. This was heavyweight, slow to iterate, and forced you to mix untested libraries into your production container. Now, with Task Runners, it's finally clean and modular.

🧩 How it works
Task Runners move code execution from the main n8n process to separate workers — either as internal child processes or fully external containers. That means:
- Better isolation and stability
- Independent resource management (scale runners separately)
- Faster iteration when adding custom dependencies
- Improved security posture

🛠️ What's even better
Since Task Runners are bundled in the n8n Docker image but run as separate processes, you can:
- Build a custom Dockerfile extending the n8n image with your own JS/TS or Python dependencies
- Run it as an external task runner attached to your existing n8n instance
- Keep your main n8n container clean while extending capabilities for advanced workloads

And if you're running n8n at scale: Task Runners work seamlessly with Queue Mode, where n8n distributes workflow execution across multiple workers — each worker gets its own task runner for true horizontal scalability.

If you're running n8n with custom code requirements, Task Runners are worth exploring.

post_text:
In Part 2 of his series on Functional Languages and the Future of Programming for the Linux Professional Institure, my O'Reilly editor Andrew Oram argues that while purely functional programming languages remain niche, their core ideas have already spread widely into mainstream languages. He quotes me and my friend and colleague Dean Wampler stating that concepts like higher-order functions, pattern matching, and closures are now standard tools even outside functional ecosystems. Functional thinking has also influenced system architecture, especially in areas like microservices and scalable design. However, strict functional principles—such as avoiding side effects—remain difficult for many developers to adopt. As a result, the future of programming is likely to be hybrid, with mainstream languages continuing to absorb functional ideas without fully embracing the paradigm.

█有品牌的工程師
早在高中時期，黃紹儒就開始經營GitHub，並陸續開啟X社群和個人網站，並使用英文發布內容，紀錄自己一路走來的成績，這也是為什麼遠在美國的Cursor團隊會邀請黃紹儒來面試，不只是因為他使用Currsor的時數在全球名列前茅，GitHub上各種專案與演講經歷，更讓黃紹儒既能開發又懂宣傳的特長被看見。
(不然我也是重度Netflix使用者啊，Netflix創辦人怎麼沒來找我拍影集)
實際攤開他的GitHub網站，高中就用JavaScript開發出網頁版Minecraft獲得關注，同時陸續複製各種遊戲，例如小精靈、神燈精靈，更開發模仿 Notion 和 Trello 的生產力工具，以及受typehere.co啟發打造的筆記工具 typehere.app。琳瑯滿目的專案，正是黃紹儒醉心於「building」的證明。

█用GitHub星星數當交換條件的家庭
黃紹儒從零開始打造產品的熱情，其實早就寫在他的 DNA 裡。
其父親、台大電機系教授黃鐘揚 Chung-Yang (Ric) Huang 曾加入矽谷新創，成為教授、組建家庭後也沒有放棄創業夢，創立了優拓資訊，黃鐘揚曾在受訪時表示：「骨子裡還是想要做出自己的產品。」黃紹儒從小耳濡目染，繼承爸爸的創業家精神，而且堅持要做自己有興趣的題目。
黃紹儒分享，爸爸曾要求自己做機器人專案，興致缺缺的他不願意聽從，只好條件交換：「爸爸說只要在GitHub拿到500顆星星，就不用做機器人。」為此黃紹儒更努力學習程式、開發產品，最後成功達到里程碑，換取父母不再干涉選題。
(其他家長是看成績單判斷小孩能力，黃家則是看GitHub星星數，這根本是工程師版「考到XX分就可以….」句型)

█新一代超能力
暫時放下學業，專注打造自己感興趣的產品的想法，已在黃紹儒心中萌芽許久。早在大二暑假，他就和黃鐘揚表達過想休學的念頭；為了能和Cursor團隊一起開發有趣的產品，即使要離鄉背井、休學也在所不惜。
尤其新創工作雖有趣也伴隨著壓力，黃紹儒在異鄉要面對隨時都可能被裁員的風險，他表示自己要學習爸爸在創業、家庭、工作三頭燒的狀況下還能「像一個石頭」一樣的定性，家庭給他的深刻影響與力量不言而喻。
除此之外，他做這一切的膽量與決心來自哪裡？當我在節目聽到黃紹儒分享自己最愛的影集是兩部經典的反英雄影集 — — 《黑袍糾察隊》和《無敵少俠》時，我猜想，也許下一個世代的超級英雄，就是要透過顛覆現狀，才能找到自我。

就像這兩部影集的主角，都曾崇拜英雄體制，但最終選擇走出自己的路。
而黃紹儒的選擇，其實也有一點這樣的影子。他沒有照著「念好書、進大公司」的安全劇本走，而是選擇休學、跳上目的未知AI列車，和世界級工程師肩並肩打造未來。

如今黃紹儒已經在GitHub上獲得超過2800顆星，是全台灣前十名的開發者，已經超過高中時爸爸給他的目標數5倍以上，現實世界裡他或許不會飛天或變身，但他與團隊用一行行程式碼，讓全世界已經超過五百萬名使用者能夠用AI賦能夢想，跨出夢想的第一步，這樣的力量，難道不就是新一代的超能力嗎？

They allow us to write code using the latest syntax and features while ensuring backward compatibility with older browsers. This enables us to embrace innovation without sacrificing compatibility.

🔧 Bundling: Managing complex codebases becomes seamless with bundling tools like Webpack. They intelligently bundle our code and dependencies into optimized bundles, reducing network requests and improving loading speed. The result? Smoother user experiences and improved performance.

🔧 Browser Synchronization: Gone are the days of manual browser refreshing! Task runners like BrowserSync enable automatic browser synchronization. As we make changes to our code, the browser instantly reloads, providing real-time feedback and saving us valuable time.

By leveraging these task runners and build tools, we unlock a world of automation and optimization. They empower us to focus on what truly matters: crafting remarkable digital experiences for our users. 🌟

Task Runners in MERN Stack Development: Streamlining Workflow Efficiency

As a MERN (MongoDB, Express.js, React, and Node.js) stack developer, managing tasks and workflows is crucial for efficient project development. Task runners simplify this process by automating repetitive tasks, enhancing productivity, and reducing errors. In this article, we'll explore task runners, their benefits, and examples relevant to MERN stack development.

What are Task Runners?

Task runners are software tools that automate tasks, such as:

- Code compilation and minification
- File watching and reloading
- Testing and linting
- Deployment and packaging

Benefits of Task Runners in MERN Stack Development

- Improved Productivity: Automate routine tasks, freeing time for core development.
- Enhanced Efficiency: Streamline workflows, reducing manual errors.
- Faster Development: Speed up build processes with concurrent task execution.

Popular Task Runners for MERN Stack

- Gulp: A popular, flexible task runner for Node.js.
- Grunt: A widely-used task runner for JavaScript projects.
- npm Scripts: A built-in task runner for Node.js projects.

author: Miguel Alho
post_text:
❓ Are you using local build tools or task runners like Cake Build, Nuke (for C#), Gulp, Grunt (JS) or any other that has the same utility for whatever stack you work in? If not, why?

I've noticed a trend over time, though some of the places I've worked over the past several years - there seems to be a drop in usage of them, and I can't necessarily put my finger on "why". Time ago, they were essential for productivity (and sanity), but that just doesn't seem to be the case anymore. There are a few things that come to mind though:

* As we've moved towards declarative builds in YAML files, there is less need to have an executable, procedural build script or task list to execute the build. In this case, the build vendor has some build model you can declare, and therefore you don't want to duplicate the effort of writing the build yourself, regardless of the possible lock-in.
* The microservice approach - small services in individual repos - may have the following effect: (1) too many repos, so setting up the build / task collection becomes overhead in each repo; (2) repos are simpler, so builds are simpler, so "something" simpler (a single script) is enough;
* Setup cost for the task colleciton is greater than copying scripts or commands, or some better way of sharing reusable bits were found, so the task manager had less benefit;
* Build definition, for whatever reason, has been offloaded to a seperate team, meaning that the tasks that would have been defined by these tools, would need to match that teams skills rather then the dev's knowledge set.

Have you seen this "trend" like I have? Or is your context the opposite?

author: Ilker Akkaya
post_text:
🤖 Van Software Testing naar AI Testing

AI-toepassingen worden steeds meer onderdeel van het softwarelandschap. Daarmee verandert ook de rol van Quality Assurance.

Bij traditionele softwaretests kunnen we voor een bepaalde input vaak een verwachte output definiëren. Bij systemen die gebaseerd zijn op LLM’s ligt dat anders: dezelfde input hoeft niet altijd exact dezelfde output op te leveren.

Daarom is alleen de vraag “Werkt het?” niet meer voldoende.

Bij het testen van AI-systemen moeten we ook kijken naar aspecten zoals factuality, relevance, hallucination, consistency, safety en response quality.

Om mijn kennis op dit gebied verder te ontwikkelen, heb ik de training LLM Evaluation (AI Testing) succesvol afgerond. 🎓

Tijdens de training heb ik mij onder andere verdiept in Promptfoo, Hugging Face, LLM-as-a-Judge, deterministic & non-deterministic evaluation, Red Team Testing en Model Auditing. LLM-Evaluation-Testing.pdf

Een belangrijk inzicht dat ik hieruit meeneem:

AI testen gaat niet alleen om controleren of een antwoord correct is. Het gaat ook om systematisch beoordelen hoe betrouwbaar, consistent, veilig en relevant een AI-systeem zich gedraagt.

Met mijn achtergrond in QA en Test Automation blijf ik mij verder ontwikkelen richting LLM Evaluation en AI Testing. 🚀

Software Testing → AI Testing

#AITesting #LLMEvaluation #QualityAssurance #SoftwareTesting #LLM #Promptfoo #RedTeaming #TestAutomation #ArtificialIntelligence #QAEngineer

MCP vs API, many people get confused.

I've explained each in simple below.

𝗠𝗢𝗗𝗘𝗟 𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗧𝗘𝗫𝗧 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗧𝗢𝗖𝗢𝗟 (𝗠𝗖𝗣)
MCP is a standard that lets AI agents discover and use tools, databases, files, and APIs through a single interface.

• 𝗘𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗮 𝘁𝗮𝘀𝗸 – Tell the AI what you want to accomplish.
• 𝗔𝗜 𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗱𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗴𝗼𝗮𝗹 – The model determines which tools are needed.
• 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗺𝘂𝗻𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝘃𝗶𝗮 𝗠𝗖𝗣 – The AI sends standardized requests instead of custom integrations.
• 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝗰𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗮𝘃𝗮𝗶𝗹𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝘁𝗼𝗼𝗹𝘀 – MCP identifies servers exposing databases, files, APIs, or other capabilities.

𝗔𝗣𝗣𝗟𝗜𝗖𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗚𝗥𝗔𝗠𝗠𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗜𝗡𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗙𝗔𝗖𝗘 (𝗔𝗣𝗜)
An API is a communication interface that lets software applications exchange data and services.

• 𝗨𝘀𝗲𝗿 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘀 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗮𝗻 𝗮𝗽𝗽 – Open a web or mobile application.

• 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗵 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗔𝗣𝗜 𝗴𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘄𝗮𝘆 – Requests are authenticated and routed.

• 𝗔𝗰𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗼𝗿 𝗲𝘅𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺𝘀 – Services interact with databases, caches, or third-party APIs.
• 𝗘𝘅𝗲𝗰𝘂𝘁𝗲 𝗯𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗹𝗼𝗴𝗶𝗰 – The backend performs the required operations.
• 𝗥𝗲𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗻 𝗮 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗽𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗲 – Data is sent back to the application.
• 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝗽𝗹𝗮𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘂𝗹𝘁 – The user sees the output in the app.
• 𝗥𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗶𝗿𝗲 𝗰𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗺 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗴𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 – Every API has its own endpoints and documentation.
• 𝗜𝗱𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘀𝗼𝗳𝘁𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 – Connects applications, services, and backend systems.

In short:
• 𝗠𝗖𝗣 → 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝗰𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿, 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗰𝘁, 𝘂𝘀𝗲 𝘁𝗼𝗼𝗹𝘀
• 𝗔𝗣𝗜 → 𝗖𝗮𝗹𝗹, 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗺𝘂𝗻𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗲, 𝗲𝘅𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮

Most people think MCP will replace APIs. The reality is, MCP makes APIs easier for AI models to discover and use.

author: Muhammad Usman Shahbaz
post_text:
7 RAG Design Patterns You Must Know in 2026.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) isn't single architecture in 2026 it will be an ecosystem of specialized patterns designed for different business needs.

Here's a quick breakdown of the 7 RAG design patterns every AI builder should know:

🔹 Naive RAG
The foundation. Retrieve relevant chunks → send to LLM → generate response. Simple, fast, but often struggles with retrieval quality.

🔹 Retrieve-and-Rerank RAG
Adds a reranking layer to improve context relevance before generation. Higher accuracy, better answers.

🔹 Multimodal RAG
Retrieves from text, images, audio, and video. Essential for enterprise knowledge bases, healthcare, retail, and media applications.

🔹 GraphRAG
Uses knowledge graphs to capture relationships between entities. Powerful for complex reasoning and connected data exploration.

🔹 Hybrid RAG
Combines vector search + graph databases. Delivers both semantic understanding and structured relationship reasoning.

🔹 Agentic RAG (Router)
An AI agent decides which data source, retrieval strategy, or tool to use. Smarter orchestration, lower hallucination risk.

🔹 Multi-Agent RAG
Multiple specialized agents collaborate on retrieval, web search, tool usage, and synthesis. Best suited for advanced enterprise AI systems.

The teams that understand these patterns today will build the most reliable AI products tomorrow.

Which RAG architecture are you currently experimenting with or planning to adopt next? | 62 comments on LinkedIn

أهلاً، أشارك معكم اليوم وحده من آخر التجارب اللي سويتها.

قاعد أستعد لواحد من الاختبارات الفترة القادمة، وواجهت مشكلة إن أغلب المصادر كانت قرائية، وإذا كان فيه كورسات فهي ما ناسبتني على المستوى الشخصي.

فقررت أسوي محتوى قرائي خاص فيني وأعتمد عليه، لكن كشخص ما يحبّذ القراءة المطوّلة كان هالشي كابوس بالنسبة لي. وأمس طرأ على بالي إني أحوّل هالمحتوى لفيديوهات فيها عناصر بصرية ومتحركة، عشان أسد الفجوة بين المكتوب وبين اللي يحاول النص يوصله.

بديت بالمحتوى نفسه قبل الفيديوهات. أطلقت مجموعة Agents عن طريق Claude Code، فيه اللي يراجع المادة العلمية، واللي يكتب نصوص الشرح، واللي يدقق كل معلومة على المصدر. وسويت فحص يتأكد إن كل نقطة في المادة لها مكان في الكورس.

الرسوم نفسها سويتها بـ Remotion، وكل رسمة مربوطة بالكلمة اللي تنقال وقتها في الشرح. وللصوت استخدمت آخر نموذج من ElevenLabs. أول عينة كان الشرح فيها سريع ومكثف واحتجت أعيدها مرتين عشان أفهم، فرجعت عدلت النصوص وخليت الشرح أهدأ وأوضح، وصرت أفحص الصوت آلياً عشان أتأكد إن ما فيه كلمة انقطعت أو انقرأت غلط.

لا يزال قيد التجربة، وبعلمكم بعد ما آخذ الاختبار بحول الله.

author: Favour Nwachukwu
post_text:
Top 25 Backend Concepts
(every serious software engineer should understand)

SYSTEM DESIGN
1. Load Balancing
↳ Distributes traffic across multiple servers.

2. Caching
↳ Stores frequently accessed data closer to the application.

3. Database Indexing
↳ Makes queries faster without scanning the entire dataset.

4. Replication
↳ Keeps copies of data across multiple nodes for availability.

5. Sharding
↳ Splits data across multiple databases when one can no longer handle the load.

DISTRIBUTED SYSTEMS

6. Eventual Consistency
↳ Allows different nodes to temporarily have different versions of data.

7. Idempotency
↳ Ensures repeating a request doesn't create unintended duplicate effects.

8. Distributed Locks
↳ Prevents multiple workers from modifying the same resource simultaneously.

9. Leader Election
↳ Allows distributed nodes to agree on which node coordinates a task.

10. Consensus
↳ Helps distributed systems agree on shared state despite failures.

PERFORMANCE and RELIABILITY

11. Backpressure
↳ Prevents fast producers from overwhelming slower consumers.

12. Rate Limiting
↳ Controls how many requests a client can make within a given period.

13. Circuit Breakers
↳ Stops repeatedly calling a failing dependency.

14. Retries
↳ Reattempts failed operations when failures are likely temporary.

15. Timeouts
↳ Prevents your system from waiting indefinitely for a dependency.

ASYNCHRONOUS SYSTEMS
16. Message Queues
↳ Decouple producers from consumers and process work asynchronously.

17. Pub/Sub
↳ Allows multiple consumers to react to the same event.

18. Dead Letter Queues
↳ Stores messages that repeatedly fail processing.

19. Consumer Groups
↳ Distributes messages across consumers for parallel processing.

20. At-Least-Once Delivery
↳ Requires you to design for duplicate messages and safe retries.

DATA and ARCHITECTURE

21. Transactions
↳ Keeps related database operations consistent.

22. Connection Pooling
↳ Reuses database connections instead of creating one per request.

23. CQRS
↳ Separates read and write models when their requirements differ.

24. Observability
↳ Uses logs, metrics, and traces to understand system behavior.

25. Disaster Recovery
↳ Defines how systems recover when infrastructure or data fails.

Don’t just memorize them.
Understand how they work together.
Save this for later.

author: Aditya Mhatre
post_text:
🚀 𝐁𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐭 𝐚𝐧 𝐞𝐧𝐝-𝐭𝐨-𝐞𝐧𝐝 𝐀𝐈-𝐩𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐝 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚 𝐈𝐧𝐜𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐈𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐠𝐚𝐭𝐨𝐫 𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐌𝐂𝐏.
Over the past few weeks, I wanted to understand Model Context Protocol (MCP) beyond basic implementations, so I built a real-world system where an AI agent can investigate failing data pipelines using operational data.

🔎 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗮: When a data pipeline fails, can an AI agent systematically investigate the incident instead of simply generating a guess?🧠
How it works:
A user can ask:
“Investigate the customer_sync pipeline and determine why it is failing.”

The LLM dynamically decides which information it needs and uses MCP tools to investigate:
• Pipeline status
• Recent pipeline runs
• Pipeline logs
• Pipeline dependencies
• Incident timelines
• Recent deployments
• Database health
The retrieved information is converted into structured evidence, maintained throughout the investigation, and used to generate a final report containing:
Summary → Severity → Confidence → Evidence → Hypotheses → Recommendations → Uncertainty

🔌 𝗔 𝗸𝗲𝘆 𝗽𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁 : I built both the MCP Client and MCP Server rather than only consuming an existing MCP server.

Working on both sides gave me a much deeper understanding of the complete MCP system , from tool discovery and invocation to tool exposure, request handling, and integration with application services and PostgreSQL.
🔍 Example
In one investigation, the agent collected evidence showing:
crm-service deployment
↓
email column returned JSONB
↓
transformation expected VARCHAR
↓
schema mismatch
↓
customer_sync failed

The final report separates evidence, hypotheses, and uncertainty rather than presenting assumptions as facts.
🏗️ 𝗔𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲
LLM → MCP Client → MCP Server → Investigation Tools → Services → PostgreSQL → Evidence → Final Report🛠️
𝗧𝗲𝗰𝗵 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗰𝗸: Python | MCP | Groq | PostgreSQL | SQLAlchemy | Docker | uv

💡 𝗕𝗶𝗴𝗴𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗮𝘄𝗮𝘆: MCP doesnt make the LLM smarter. It provides a standardized way for an AI application to discover and interact with external tools and data.Building this project helped me understand that concept by actually implementing the system end-to-end.

이번 프로그램에서는 기획파트장 정건님께서는 AI-native한 기획 방식을 함께 단련시키고자 합니다. 해결하려는 문제와 판단 근거를 기록하고, 그 기록을 바탕으로 AI와 함께 결과물을 만든 뒤 직접 검증하는 방식입니다. 무엇을 만들고, 어떤 내용을 바꾸고, 결과가 의도에 맞는지는 기획자가 판단해야 합니다.

앞으로는 기획자가 직접 작동하는 프로토타입을 만들고 디자인·개발 팀과 함께 검토하는 과정까지 다뤄보려고 합니다. 첫 주차를 함께 준비해주신 SOPT 운영진과 참여해주신 기획파트 여러분께 감사합니다.

We kicked off our first Codex session with the product planning team of SOPT’s 39th cohort in Korea.

SOPT is a university student tech and startup community where product planners, designers, and engineers form teams to build real products. I’m participating as an OpenAI Codex Ambassador, helping product planners explore how Codex can fit into their work.

In the first session, we covered a concrete workflow: document a team discussion, have Codex read those notes and research materials, and create an HTML presentation draft. Then open the actual file, check the content and layout, and revise it.

author: Jim Jansen
post_text:
Assessing inter-rater agreement among large language model judges: Evidence from persona evaluation across varying educational risk contexts

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed as automated judges for evaluation, yet their reliability remains unclear.

In this research, led by Danial Amin, this study examines the inter-rater agreement of three LLM judges (GPT-4o, Claude 3 Sonnet, and Gemini 1.5 Pro) when evaluating fairness, lack of stereotypicality, and diversity in user personas across varying educational risk contexts.

We analyzed 60 individual personas and 12 persona sets to assess whether these judges demonstrate sufficient consistency to function as reliable evaluators.

Although inter-rater agreement was moderate at the individual persona level, three critical limitations emerged.

At the set level, agreement ranged from .39 to .63 across persona generators and therefore did not show a uniform decline relative to individual-level agreement. Mean dimension-support scores were 41% to 61% lower, although the individual- and set-level tasks are not directly comparable.

Second, non-compliance rates, where judges could not provide textual justification for their ratings, ranged from 9.6 to 26.7% at the individual level and increased to 34% to 49% at the set level.

Third, agreement differed across the three educational scenarios classified by risk: individual-level agreement declined from the lower- to higher-risk scenarios, while set-level agreement showed no monotonic pattern. We conclude that, under the tested protocol, current LLM judges demonstrate poor-to-moderate inter-rater agreement for persona evaluation.

These findings provide a descriptive characterization of LLM evaluation behavior across risk contexts and lay the foundation for future validation studies comparing LLM agreement with human judgment.

Amin, D., Salminen, J., and Jansen, B. J. (2027) Assessing Inter-Rater Agreement Among Large Language Model Judges: Evidence from Persona Evaluation Across Varying Educational Risk Contexts, Technological Forecasting amp; Social Change. Article: 124894,

author: Roberto Heckers
post_text:
Did you know ng new, even in strict mode, leaves one of the most useful #TypeScript flags off? 👀

noUncheckedIndexedAccess. One line in tsconfig.json.

Without it, TypeScript tells you orders[0] is an Order. It is not. It is an Order, or undefined when the array is empty. Same for a Record lookup with a key nobody ever set. The type lies, the code reads fine, and the production error says "Cannot read properties of undefined".

With the flag on, every index read becomes T | undefined. You add a ?. or an early return, and that bug can no longer compile ✅

The flag reaches further than most people expect: it applies inside your #Angular templates too. The template type checker generates plain TypeScript from your template, so it inherits every compiler option. orders()[0].id in an interpolation or o.lines[0].sku inside an @for block fails the build with TS2532, the same error you would get in the class.

Angular's extended diagnostics account for it as well. With the flag off, the compiler deliberately stays quiet about a fallback on an indexed read like items[0], because it knows the non-nullable type cannot be trusted there. With it on, the type is honest and the diagnostics can be too.

Turning it on in an existing codebase costs an afternoon. Most fixes are a question mark. A few are real bugs you did not know you had, and those pay for the afternoon.

One of the greatest parts of GitHub Copilot is the wide variety of models available to perform a task. But...one of the biggest challenges with Copilot is knowing which model is most appropriate for a given task.

I've listened to many strong developers admit they regularly use only one (or perhaps two) models no matter the task at hand. Sometimes this is because people like always using the most powerful tool no matter how small the job... like using an F-250 to haul a single bag of mulch. But often it's because there are simply so many choices, that change so frequently, that it's unreasonable to expect everyone to keep up.

At GitHub we've been iterating on making an "easy" button for this for a while. Recently we updated how Auto mode works by giving developers the option to choose to optimize for efficiency, balance, or intelligence.

LLM evaluation is where you find out if your model is actually good, or just sounds good.

A model can write impressive answers and still fail on accuracy, reasoning, consistency, safety, or hallucinations.

That’s why evaluating an LLM goes beyond asking, “Does this answer look good?”
You need to test things like:
• Accuracy
• Relevance
• Reasoning
• Factuality
• Hallucination
• Safety
• Consistency
• Instruction following
And depending on the use case, you might use benchmarks, human evaluation, LLM-as-a-judge, or custom evaluation datasets.

Building an LLM is only half the job. Knowing whether it actually works is the other half.

author: Himanshu Agarwal
post_text:
MCP Architecture — The Missing Layer Between AI and Real-World Systems

AI models are powerful.

But an LLM alone cannot directly understand your databases, APIs, files, cloud services, internal tools, or enterprise systems.

That’s where Model Context Protocol (MCP) comes in.

MCP provides a standardized way for AI applications to connect with external tools and data.

The basic architecture:

AI Application / MCP Client
↓
MCP Protocol — JSON-RPC 2.0
↓
MCP Server
↓
Tools + Resources + Prompts
↓
Databases | APIs | Files | Cloud | SaaS | Custom Systems

A typical flow looks like:

1. Client sends a request
2. MCP server receives the request
3. Server invokes the required tool or resource
4. External system processes the request
5. Structured result is returned
6. LLM uses the result to generate the final response

For AI Test Engineers, MCP introduces an entirely new testing surface:

• Tool invocation validation
• JSON-RPC request/response validation
• Schema validation
• Authentication & authorization testing
• Prompt injection testing
• Tool poisoning testing
• Access-control testing
• Error handling & timeout testing
• Data leakage testing
• MCP server reliability testing

MCP is not just an AI integration concept.

It is becoming an important architecture layer for building and testing AI-powered systems.

Save this architecture for your MCP + AI Testing journey.

author: Ashok Kumar Sitha
post_text:
What is MCP(Model Context Protocol)

* MCP is a standard way for AI to connect with external tools and data.
* Think of MCP as a universal adapter between an AI model and different systems.
* Without MCP, every AI application may need a custom integration for each tool.
* With MCP, the AI can use a common protocol to connect to databases, APIs, files, applications, and other tools.
* The MCP Server exposes the available tools/data to the AI and handles communication with those systems.
* This allows AI to not only understand information, but also retrieve data and perform actions.

Simple example

User: “Find the latest sales data and create a report.”

AI → MCP → Database/Tools → MCP → AI → Report

¿Crees que un contenedor comprometido no puede tocar tu servidor? 🐳
Una nueva vulnerabilidad de Docker, CVE-2026-17106 (CopyEscape), pone el foco en una frontera que muchas veces damos por aislada:
contenedor → host
La vulnerabilidad afecta a docker cp y puede permitir que archivos sean escritos fuera del directorio de destino esperado.
🔎 Revisé mi propio entorno y tenía Docker Engine 29.5.2, dentro del rango afectado.
Lo actualicé a 29.8.2 y quedó corregido.
Si usas Docker, revisa primero:
docker version
Y actualiza Docker Engine desde el repositorio oficial de tu distribución:
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade
o, según tu distribución:
sudo dnf upgrade docker-ce
Después, vuelve a comprobar:
docker version
⚠️ No revises solamente tus imágenes. El Docker Engine, runners de CI/CD y operaciones que cruzan hacia el host también forman parte de la superficie de ataque.
Si utilizas docker cp en pipelines o automatizaciones, vale la pena revisarlo.

author: Harshad Bhatt
post_text:
My first ever system design interview was for HDFC Bank and it went so terribly that I still remember almost every minute of it.

The problem was simple on paper: Design a notification system.

I had watched tutorials, so I immediately drew a high-level diagram on the screen. Big boxes for queues, services, and databases. I thought I was doing fine.

Then the interviewer asked me to go deeper:
- "Walk me through the exact data flow step-by-step."
- "Show me the classes, schema, and API boundaries."

I froze.

I couldn't write the classes. I couldn't trace the actual flow of data. I had memorized the high-level architecture boxes, but I had zero idea how to actually break down the lower-level mechanics.

The worst part? It was a 60-minute interview, and for the remaining 45 minutes, he kept pushing and grilling me to work through it, even though it was obvious to both of us that I had no idea what I was doing.

It was uncomfortable and exhausting. But honestly, those 45 minutes taught me more than any video lecture ever had.

That failure completely changed how I approached system design from that day on:
-> HLD without LLD is just guesswork: If you draw a message queue, you need to know what payload goes into it, who consumes it, and how failures get handled.

-> Stop memorizing boxes and arrows: An interview isn't about drawing an entire microservice ecosystem. It's about data models, API contracts, and trade-offs.

-> Embrace the discomfort: Getting stuck in an interview is normal. Learning to think out loud, ask clarifying questions, and break a problem down methodically is the real skill.

Looking back, that brutal 45 minutes at HDFC was the exact reality check I needed. It reshaped my preparation, taught me how to actually communicate during design rounds, and ultimately helped me clear my loops at Visa

Every engineer has had at least one interview that completely humbled them.

What was the one interview failure that taught you the most? Drop it below. 👇

author: Guillermo Rauch

DHH is fundamentally right about Rust. For context, Vercel has been undergoing a Rust-ification (carcinization, technically 🦀) for a while.

One of the first projects we migrated was Turborepo, from Go to Rust¹. The migration completed, but the RoI was actually quite controversial internally.

While Rust was in our eyes better for low-level OS access, something crucial for a build system like Turbo, the human migration costs were very substantive.

Go is very fast. It's beautifully designed. It's easy to iterate on. We were very conflicted about the migration, because it was *humans* writing the code, *even if we knew Rust was a better choice*.

The calculus has now changed. What's "best for humans" is no longer necessarily "best for business".

FWIW, it's also quite unlikely that Rust is the end-all-be-all toolchain. I'm quite certain there's greener pasture ahead, because Rust itself was designed before the 'supersonic tsunami' of agents hit.

You can write C++ every day and not have memory issues ... for years. It's not hard.

• Train or fine-tune an LLM — we've got to a point where doing this, even on your local machine is so easy. The resources are overwhelming and the tools (Prime Intellect, Tinker and Unsloth) are very nice to use. And it really puts into perspective how all these modern LLMs operate.

• Make a game in a Fantasy Console — programs like PICO-8 or TIC-80 are really fun, have real constraints and challenge you a lot to work within bounds. It makes you think and system design and optimize for efficiency as much as possible.

• Experiment with Music — this could be with physical instruments or even digital synthesizers. There are even tools like Strudel that let you make music through code. Music really opens up your eyes to a whole new universe. It's really fun.

• Make Pixel Art — there are a lot of good softwares specialized for pixel art like Aseprite so use them to draw some unique quirky art. Really shows you how valuable good art is.

• Run simulations in Python — there are so many things you can simulate using python. From gravity to ant colonies, from solar systems to population data. It's extremely fun visualizing interactions and seeing the effects.

These are just a few, there's a lot you can do in the digital world. Don't lock yourself up in a single window and be bored. There are endless things you will love doing and trying out in the digital world. Enjoy!

author: Srikant Mahanty
post_text:
Your PostgreSQL query is slow.

Developer: “Just add an index.” 😎

PostgreSQL: “Sure… but who is going to pay for it?” 😂

Indexes are powerful, but they are not free.

They speed up reads, but add storage, write overhead, WAL, maintenance, and sometimes… absolutely nothing.

Take this:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM users
WHERE is_active = true;
```

95% of users are active.

You add an index on `is_active`.

PostgreSQL looks at it and says:

“Why should I walk through the index to find almost the whole table?” 😂

Sometimes a sequential scan is simply cheaper.

Now imagine a write-heavy event table receiving millions of inserts.

You add 6 indexes because “these columns are used in queries.”

Every insert now has more work.

The read query got faster.

The write path got slower.

And then someone asks:

“Why is ingestion latency increasing?” 😶

Same story with frequently updated columns:

```sql
UPDATE sessions
SET last_seen = now();
```

If `last_seen` is indexed and changes constantly, congratulations — you just created extra index maintenance for every update. 😅

Even small tables can make an index unnecessary.

And large text columns? Don't blindly index them either. Maybe you actually need full-text search or a GIN index.

So before saying:

“Add an index.”

Ask:

→ How selective is this column?
→ How big is the table?
→ Read-heavy or write-heavy?
→ How often does the value change?
→ What does `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` say?

Because database optimization is not:

“More indexes = more performance.”

It is:

“Right index + right query + right workload.”

Sometimes the best index…

is no index. 😄

author: Animesh Mishra
post_text:
Python 3.15 is a big one. And the headline feature fixes a problem every Python dev has felt: slow startup.

Python 3.15 adds explicit lazy imports (PEP 810) with a new lazy keyword. Python skips the load and creates a lightweight proxy. The module loads on first use. No more imports buried inside functions just to save startup time.
A few details worth knowing:
🔹 Lazy imports only work at module scope. Using lazy inside a function, class, or try/except raises a SyntaxError.
🔹 Star imports can't be lazy.
🔹 If a lazy import fails, the error appears at first use, with a traceback pointing to the original import line.
🔹 Need to support older Python versions? Define __lazy_modules__ instead.
🔹 You can also enable it globally with -X lazy_imports=all or the PYTHON_LAZY_IMPORTS environment variable.
But there's more in 3.15:
✅ frozendict is a new built-in immutable dict. It's hashable if its keys and values are.
✅ sentinel is a new built-in for creating unique sentinel values (PEP 661).
✅ Unpacking in comprehensions: [*L for L in lists] replaces nested comprehensions and itertools.chain.
✅ UTF-8 is now the default encoding, regardless of your system locale. Add an explicit encoding= to your open() calls anyway.
✅ Tachyon, a new sampling profiler in the profiling package. It can attach to a running process with near-zero overhead, with no restart needed. It's great for production debugging.
✅ Smarter error messages. [1, 2, 3].push(4) now suggests .append, and 'hello'.toUpperCase() suggests .upper. Nice for devs coming from JavaScript.
✅ Typing upgrades: TypeForm (PEP 747) and TypedDict with typed extra items (PEP 728).
✅ Upgraded experimental JIT and a stable ABI for free-threaded builds.
✅ More color across the CLI tools.

Heads-up: the incremental garbage collector from 3.14 has been reverted to the generational GC, after reports of memory pressure in production.

If you maintain a large app or CLI tool, lazy imports alone could noticeably cut your startup time. I'm planning to test it on my own projects.

You can publish 100 UGC videos and learn absolutely nothing. Here's how to make sure that doesn't happen.

If every video tests a different creator, hook, angle, format, AND way of showing the product, you have no idea why one worked and another didn’t.

By the way: I’m Julia, co-founder of Playkit. Since 2024, we’ve driven 12M+ app downloads and 1B+ organic views for Cash App, Quizlet, Substack, Grubhub, and more.

I’m sharing a free course on UGC for consumer apps. This is lesson 4, and it’s about planning your first 100 videos.

The goal of those first 100 videos is to figure out which combinations are worth making more of.

For context, we analyzed 69,000+ UGC videos and found that videos with more than 500K views made up just 0.3% of the total, but drove more than half of all views.

You need enough attempts to find those outliers, but volume only helps if you know what you are learning from it.

I would test five things intentionally:

1. Angles
2. Formats
3. Hooks
4. Creators
5. Product integration

I broke down what each one means, what to change, and what you are actually trying to learn from it in the carousel.

One other thing: I would NOT plan all 100 videos upfront.

The first batch should change the second, the second should change the third, etc.

By video 100, you should have fewer guesses than you started with.

author: Gaurav Goyal
post_text:
Not every AI agent needs the same architecture.

Some agents simply call a tool.
Some make a plan before acting.
Some review their own answers.
Some work with other agents.
And some need a human in the loop.

That’s why understanding agent patterns is more useful than memorizing a single definition of “AI agent.”

Here are 8 patterns I keep coming across in real-world agentic systems:

1️⃣ ReAct — Reason → Act → Observe
2️⃣ Tool Calling — Use external tools and APIs
3️⃣ Planning — Break complex work into steps
4️⃣ Reflection — Review and improve the output
5️⃣ Multi-Agent — Multiple agents with different roles
6️⃣ Router — Send requests to the right agent/model
7️⃣ Human-in-the-Loop — Human feedback or approval
8️⃣ Memory — Maintain useful context over time

And the interesting part?

You can combine these patterns.

A production system could use a Router + Planner + Tools + Memory + Human approval.

The LLM is only one piece.

The architecture around the LLM is what makes the agent useful.

post_text:
Most lessons-learned posts focus on what we would do differently. I was reflecting on a call from yesterday, and I think sometimes I would rather celebrate what went well. 🎉

After a year and a half of building an interactive implementation guide with Solutions for Kids in Pain (SKIP), the tool we co-created has launched and is now live. We had a wrap-up meeting to debrief about the process with Kathryn (Katie) Birnie, PhD RPsych, Valentina Gastaldo, and the SKIP team.

Here are some of my takeaways from this incredible partnership were:

🤝 Strong relationships were central to our success. When plans changed, which they frequently did, the fact that we trusted each other seems like the most important element of this partnership.
🎨 Uncertainty made us more creative. We all needed to accept that for fairly long periods of time, there was a lot of uncertainty. It was that uncertainty that actually allowed all of us to be creative in our own ways. Literally every element of this toolkit was built more creatively because we didn't know exactly where it was going: the way the pain domains content was crafted, the way implementation science was woven in, and the software that was used to make the tool have the functionality it does.

post_text:
RAG Design Patterns Every LLM Engineer Should Know

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is more than:
"Chunk → Embed → Search → Generate"

In production systems, retrieval quality and architecture often determine the quality of the final answer.

Here are some important RAG design patterns:

1. Naive RAG
Documents → Chunking → Embeddings → Vector Search → LLM

Simple and useful for getting started, but can struggle with complex queries and noisy retrieval.

2. Hybrid RAG

Combines:
- Keyword search
- Vector search
- Semantic similarity

Useful when both exact terms and semantic meaning matter.

3. Query Transformation
User Query → Query Rewriting → Retrieval → LLM

The system reformulates the original query to improve retrieval quality.

4. Multi-Query RAG
One user question → Multiple search queries → Multiple retrieval results → Reranking → LLM

Useful when a question can be interpreted from multiple perspectives.

5. Reranking Pattern
Query → Initial Retrieval → Reranker → Top-K Context → LLM

A reranker improves the relevance of retrieved documents before they reach the model.

6. Parent-Child Retrieval
Small chunks are used for precise retrieval, while larger parent documents provide additional context to the LLM.

7. Contextual Retrieval
Instead of embedding isolated chunks, additional document context is added before indexing.

This can improve retrieval when individual chunks lack sufficient context.

8. Agentic RAG
Query → Agent → Retrieval/Tools → Reasoning → Final Answer

The agent decides when and how to retrieve information instead of following a fixed retrieval pipeline.

9. Graph RAG
Documents → Entities & Relationships → Knowledge Graph → Retrieval → LLM

Useful for questions requiring relationships across entities and documents.

10. Corrective RAG
Retrieve → Evaluate Retrieved Context → Correct/Retry Retrieval → Generate

The system checks retrieval quality and performs additional retrieval when the initial results are insufficient.

A practical production RAG architecture can look like:

User Query
↓
Query Understanding
↓
Query Transformation
↓
Hybrid Retrieval
↓
Reranking
↓
Context Filtering
↓
LLM
↓
Evaluation & Guardrails
↓
Response

The key lesson:
RAG is not a single technique.

It is a collection of design patterns that can be combined depending on the data, query complexity, latency requirements, accuracy expectations, and cost constraints.

Good RAG design starts with understanding the retrieval problem—not simply choosing a vector database.

author: Oren Melamed
post_text:
Agent Bakeoff is coming to GitHub Copilot.

Instead of running the same task manually with different models, you can now run multiple agent attempts and compare the results side by side.

You can run 2-10 attempts, use different models, or even run the same model multiple times.

Each attempt gets its own isolated worktree, while the workspace, harness, execution mode, permissions and other task configuration stay consistent.

Then you can add a Judge to evaluate the attempts and a Synthesizer to combine the results.

So:

Task → multiple agent runs → Judge → Synthesis

There is also telemetry around the comparison, including the comparison ID and the role of each participant.

What I find more interesting is how this fits with some of the other things landing in Copilot right now that I recently wrote about.

HydraFusion is exploring how Copilot can dynamically choose a workflow and coordinate multiple models within a turn.

Dynamic Workflows go in almost the opposite direction: you define the process - the steps, conditions, handoffs, parallelism and checkpoints - and agents execute the parts that need reasoning.

And Agent Bakeoff gives you a way to experiment with the execution itself and compare the outcomes.

So I don't see these as three competing features at all.

I see them as different pieces of the same direction:

Define the process. Choose or discover how to execute it. Run multiple approaches. Evaluate the results.

That's a much more interesting direction than simply adding another model to the picker. I think this is where @GitHubCopilot really shines vs other harnesses especially lately with all of these features.

𝐌𝐂𝐏 𝐢𝐬𝐧’𝐭 𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭 𝐚 𝐰𝐚𝐲 𝐭𝐨 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐧𝐞𝐜𝐭 𝐚𝐧 𝐀𝐈 𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐨 𝐭𝐨𝐨𝐥𝐬. 𝐈𝐭 𝐝𝐞𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐬 𝐚 𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞𝐝 𝐰𝐚𝐲 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐀𝐈 𝐬𝐲𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐦𝐬 𝐭𝐨 𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐜𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫, 𝐚𝐜𝐜𝐞𝐬𝐬, 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐞𝐱𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐚𝐥 𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐞𝐬.

𝐀𝐬 𝐀𝐈 𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐛𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞, 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐧𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐦 𝐭𝐨 𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐥-𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐥𝐝 𝐬𝐲𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐦𝐬 𝐛𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐬 𝐚 𝐦𝐚𝐣𝐨𝐫 𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐞𝐧𝐠𝐞.

That’s where Model Context Protocol (MCP) comes in.

At a high level, MCP connects an AI application to external systems through three core capabilities:

→ Tools → Let the model perform actions such as API calls, database queries, file operations, or custom actions.

→ Resources → Provide read-only data and context such as files, documents, database records, knowledge bases, or application state.

→ Prompts → Provide reusable templates for tasks, workflows, analysis, or domain-specific instructions.

The architecture is built around a few important layers:

→ Host → The AI application or agent that manages the user interaction.

→ MCP Client → Handles protocol communication and manages the connection.

→ Transport → Carries messages between client and server through mechanisms such as stdio or Streamable HTTP.

→ MCP Server → Exposes tools, resources, and prompts to the application.

→ External Systems → APIs, databases, file systems, SaaS tools, and business systems.

The interaction follows a clear lifecycle:

Initialize → Negotiate → Establish Session → Discover → Invoke / Read → Return Result → Continue → Close

And security matters at every layer.

→ Authentication → Verify users and services

→ Authorization → Control what can be accessed

→ Capability-level access → Restrict specific tools and resources

→ Data protection → Control sensitive information

→ Auditing → Monitor tool usage and unusual activity

The biggest idea is that MCP standardizes the interaction protocol, not your entire application.

You still design:

→ Application logic

→ Authentication and authorization

→ Permissions

→ Which capabilities to expose

→ External system integrations

→ Monitoring and governance

The key takeaway

MCP gives AI applications a standardized and modular way to connect with real-world tools, data, and systems.

The protocol provides the structure.

You still design the boundaries.

Save this for your next MCP, AI agent, or LLM application project.

Introducing gdp-ts: Ghosts of Departed Proofs for TypeScript.

gdp-ts is a library, linter and AI skill for safer API design. Under this contract, sensitive functions require 'proofs' that the caller performed an authorization check.

The typechecker verifies these proofs at compile time, preventing your team and agents from shipping catastrophic security (and other kinds of) bugs.

While these patterns have existed for quite some time, especially in ecosystems like Haskell, ① human code review and ② cognitive and syntactic overhead made these solutions niche.

The situation is now inverted. Agents are writing more code than we can review, and they *thrive* in tight loops with hard constraints that would frustrate us. We see this with the rise of Rust, borrow checker, code aesthetics debate and all.

The README and examples model a real-world Vercel API product constraint: changing the password on a Project requires a proof of a certain role + a certain entitlement. Thanks to Matt Noonan and Ollie Charles for their research in this space.

author: Michael Drogalis
post_text:
This week I learned all about Java Lambda functions. I know they're kind of old, but if you learned Java pre-8 like me, they look a bit scary at first.

Because Java is statically typed and designed with the idea that "everything is a class", it ships 5 main interfaces for implementing functions: Function, Consumer, Supplier, Runnable, and Predicate.

Which you choose depends on the function signature you need:

1. Function: takes input, returns output
2. Consumer: takes input, returns no output
3. Supplier: takes no input, returns output
4. Runnable: takes no input and gives no output (for side effects)
5. Predicate: takes input, always returns a boolean

On top of that, Java gives us a rare bit of syntactic sugar for implementing them:

• zero-parameter function: () -> "hello world"
• single parameter function, type inferred: (x) -> x * 8
• multi-parameter function: (x1, x2) -> x2 - x1
• multi-line function body: () -> { someCall(); return otherFunction(); }
• typed parameter function: (String x) -> x.charAt(42)
• passing a function by name: stream.filter(MyClass::myPredicate)

Notice two things:

1. When the body of a function is a single expression, you can ditch the braces. The expression becomes the return value.

2. Specifying parameter types is optional. The compiler can infer them for you. | 18 comments on LinkedIn

author: Chandra Sekhar
post_text:
Most RAG systems fail not because retrieval is bad, but because the architecture doesn't match the question.
⠀
Here are 9 RAG architectures and when each one earns its place 👇
⠀
1. 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗮𝗿𝗱 𝗥𝗔𝗚 — your baseline for simple fact lookup. Tune chunk size first.
2. 𝗗𝗲𝗲𝗽𝗥𝗔𝗚 — split multi-hop questions into sub-questions before retrieving.
3. 𝗠𝗔-𝗥𝗔𝗚 — specialist agents for planning, extraction and synthesis.
4. 𝗖𝗼𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗥𝗔𝗚 — answer, detect errors, retrieve again, fix.
5. 𝗦𝗽𝗲𝗰𝘂𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗥𝗔𝗚 — small model drafts, large model verifies. Fast and safe.
6. 𝗙𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗥𝗔𝗚 — multiple queries merged with Reciprocal Rank Fusion.
7. 𝗥𝗔𝗚-𝗚𝘆𝗺 — supervise each reasoning and search step, not only the final answer.
8. 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗹𝗮𝗿 𝗥𝗔𝗚 — swap the reranker or rewriter without rebuilding the pipeline.

author: Rathnakumar Udayakumar
post_text:
One architecture can explain almost every AI agent.

Behind the interface, an agent is really a continuous loop of understanding, reasoning, acting, checking, and learning.

A typical architecture looks like this:

→ Perception parses the request and identifies intent
→ Context assembly retrieves relevant knowledge and memory
→ The reasoning engine decides the next best action
→ Planning breaks the goal into smaller, ordered steps
→ Policy gates check permissions, risk, and approval requirements
→ Tools execute actions across APIs, databases, code, files, or MCP servers
→ Observations capture results and update the agent’s state
→ Reflection checks whether the outcome actually meets the goal
→ Memory stores useful context for future steps and future tasks
→ Response synthesis prepares the final output for the user

The important part is that this does not happen only once.

The agent loops through reasoning, action, observation, and reflection until the task is complete, the budget is exhausted, or a stopping condition is reached.

Two layers support the entire system:

Guardrails keep actions safe and controlled.

Observability tracks traces, logs, latency, cost, metrics, and evaluations.

That is what separates a simple chatbot from a production-ready AI agent.

The LLM is only one component.

The real power comes from the system built around it.

🏦 JPMorganChase System Design Interview: Questions Candidates Commonly Report

Preparing for a Software Engineer / Backend Engineer interview at JPMorgan Chase?

Based on system-design topics and questions commonly shared by candidates, interviews can cover a mix of HLD, LLD, Java concurrency, scalability, reliability, and data consistency.

Here are some important questions worth preparing for 👇

🔹 Low-Level Design (LLD / OOD)

• Design a Parking Lot System.
• Design an ATM / Banking System with accounts, transactions, and fund transfers.

• Which Design Pattern would you use here, and why?

• How would you apply SOLID Principles to your design?
• How would you make your design extensible for future requirements?
• How would you handle concurrent operations in your design?

• Design a Payment Processing System that prevents duplicate charges.
• Design a Ledger / Double-Entry Bookkeeping System.
• Design a Real-Time Fraud Detection Pipeline.
• Design a Notification Service supporting Email, SMS, and Push Notifications.

[ALERTS → ANALYSIS → SEVERITY → EVIDENCE → RUNBOOK → ACTION PLAN]

→ 🔍 Reliability analysis
→ 🚀 Release/change correlation
→ ⚡ Performance analysis

→ 🎯 Action prioritization
It evaluates signals such as:
• Error-rate spikes
• Latency degradation
• Threshold violations
• Multiple affected services

Then instead of simply saying:

It produces:
WHY is this happening?
WHAT evidence supports it?
WHAT should the engineer investigate next?
WHICH runbook applies?

The AI does NOT automatically execute destructive remediation.
It creates a proposed action plan and keeps execution behind a human approval boundary.
