☎️ 🇦🇪 🇨🇾 AI|Telephony: 3CX speaks MCP in two directions | Client & Server
Just made a short video explaining what Model Context Protocol means for 3CX. The idea is simple: your PBX can publish tools for AI clients, and it can use tools from other systems.

One protocol gives both sides a common way to discover and call tools.

How does this work in practice?
➕ 3CX as a server exposes permitted PBX tools.
➕ AI clients from OpenAI Anthropic Gemini Grok can check calls, queues, contacts and reports.
➕ 3CX as a client connects to external MCP servers example Salesforce HubSpot Zapier n8n
➕ A configured agent can look up a customer in Salesforce.
➕ It can create a HubSpot ticket during a call.
➕ It can trigger workflows through n8n or Zapier.
➕ User permissions and tool approvals control access.

APIs still do the underlying work. But MCP makes those capabilities easier for compatible systems to find and use.

author: Christophe Pettus
post_text:
Chris van Eijk published measurements on October 1 of what row-level security costs on PostgreSQL 17.10, on a table of two million invoices across 1,000 tenants of very unequal size. The headline is that a simple policy is free: tenant_id = nullif(current_setting('app.tenant_id', true), '')::uuid matched the non-RLS baseline almost exactly. The cost comes from how the policy is written, and three of the ways it goes wrong are common.

A helper function left at the default VOLATILE is the dramatic one. An SQL function gets inlined and stays fast; a PL/pgSQL function cannot be inlined, so VOLATILE means it is called per row and the index becomes unusable. The count went from 0.20 ms to 1,860 ms, for a tenant with 534 invoices. STABLE fixes it. So does wrapping the call in (select ...), which is the advice you usually see, and which is unnecessary for an inlinable SQL function. Two common hardening habits, SECURITY DEFINER and a SET search_path clause, break inlining and bring the problem back. Declaring the helper STABLE makes you independent of all of it.

The one to actually worry about is the leakproof rule. PostgreSQL enforces policy conditions before any query condition containing a non-leakproof function, to avoid leaking rows through error messages. lower() is not leakproof. Neither is LIKE. So where lower(customer_email) = lower($1) uses the index for tenant_id only and then filters every one of that tenant's rows. Measured: 0.21 ms without RLS, 34 to 45 ms with it for the largest tenant, and 0.38 ms for the median tenant. The cost scales with tenant size, which means it lands entirely on your biggest customer and a test database full of small tenants will never show it. A stored generated column holding lower(customer_email) with an index on (tenant_id, customer_email_lower) brought it back to 0.25 ms.

author: Raju Dandigam
post_text:
AI Agent Architecture 2026, simplified.

Building an AI agent is no longer about connecting an LLM to a chatbot.

A production-ready agent needs an entire system working behind it.

It starts with the user goal: the outcome the agent is expected to achieve. From there, the architecture expands into multiple connected layers.

→ Interface & Channels
Chat UI, APIs, Slack, or Teams become the entry points where users interact with the agent.

→ Planning & Orchestration
Frameworks like LangGraph, CrewAI, Mastra, and AutoGen help break goals into tasks, coordinate steps, and manage execution.

→ Memory & Context
Short-term memory, long-term memory, retrieval, vector databases, and prompt caching keep the agent grounded across interactions.

→ Models
Claude, GPT, Gemini, and Llama provide the reasoning layer powering decisions and responses.

→ Tools & Actions
GitHub, browsers, APIs, databases, and code execution allow agents to move from answering to actually doing work.

→ State & Data
PostgreSQL, Redis, object storage, and vector databases maintain persistent operational data.

→ Observability & Safety
Tracing, evaluation, guardrails, and quality checks help teams understand what the agent is doing and where it fails.

→ Deployment & Infrastructure
Docker, Kubernetes, cloud platforms, and edge infrastructure make the system scalable and reliable.

The real shift is simple:

AI agents are becoming software systems, not standalone models.

And designing the surrounding architecture well is what turns a clever prototype into a dependable production agent. | 78 comments on LinkedIn

Here’s a practical Python roadmap for Data & AI professionals.

Python covers a huge ecosystem, but learning it becomes much easier when the concepts are approached in the right order.

Start with the foundation:

→ Syntax, variables, data types, operators, conditions, loops, and exceptions
→ Lists, tuples, dictionaries, sets, strings, iterators, and generators
→ Functions, parameters, modules, packages, and virtual environments
→ Classes, objects, inheritance, dataclasses, context managers, and type hints

Then move into working with real data:

→ File handling with CSV, JSON, YAML, Parquet, and Pathlib
→ NumPy for arrays, vectorization, broadcasting, indexing, and numerical computing
→ Pandas for cleaning, joins, missing values, time series, and aggregations
→ Matplotlib, Seaborn, and Plotly for visualization and storytelling

From there, the path depends on your career direction.

For Data Engineering:
SQLAlchemy, ETL pipelines, Airflow, PySpark, APIs, PostgreSQL, and cloud storage.

For AI & Machine Learning:
Scikit-learn, feature engineering, model evaluation, PyTorch, Hugging Face, embeddings, and RAG.

The key is to combine learning with projects.

Build scripts, clean datasets, call APIs, create pipelines, train models, and automate repetitive tasks.

Python mastery comes from applying these concepts repeatedly, not memorizing every library.

author: Jean Malaquias
post_text:
Enterprise AI Agent Architecture: How Production-Ready Agentic AI systems actually work.

This reference architecture shows how enterprise AI agent systems securely orchestrate reasoning, RAG retrieval, memory, multi-agent collaboration, and tool execution - turning a user request into a trusted response.

Here is the end-to-end process orchestration:

0. Governance & Safety Layer:

Guardrails, PII/content safety, human-in-the-loop, and audit trail runs alongside every stage, not just at the end.

1. User / Channel:

Users interact through web, mobile, chat, or APIs to submit requests.

2. Agent Orchestrator (Control Plane):

Coordinates the workflow by planning tasks, routing requests, managing execution, and handling failures.

3. Multi-Agent Framework:

A supervisor delegates to specialist agents (research, planning, execution, review) working toward one goal.

4. Reasoning Engine (LLM):

The core brain - reasons, selects tools, and calls functions.
Analyzes the request, reasons over context, and generates intelligent decisions.

5. Memory Layer:

Maintains session context, long-term knowledge, and user preferences for personalized responses.

6. RAG (Knowledge Layer):

Retrieves and reranks relevant enterprise knowledge to ground the LLM’s answers.

7. Tools & Actions Layer:

Executes real-world actions such as search, APIs, workflows, analytics, and code execution.

8. MCP Gateway:

Provides a secure, standardized interface for AI agents to communicate with enterprise systems and tools with rate limiting and caching.

9. Identity & Policy:

Authenticates agents/users and enforces per-tool, per-data access policy at the gateway.Enforces least-privilege access, policies, and permissions.

10. Observability & Operations:

Continuously monitors reliability, performance, cost, latency, logs, and and alerting across the whole system.

11. Evaluation & Feedback Loop:

Measures response quality, captures user feedback, and continuously improves the AI system over time.

12. Final Response Delivery:
The answer is delivered with citations, confidence score, back to the right user/channel.

author: Dr Milan Milanović
post_text:
MCP, A2A and ACP connect an AI agent to three different things

AI agents today connect to different resources, and for that they use different protocols. The most important ones are MCP, A2A and ACP.

Here is what they do:

𝟭. 𝗠𝗖𝗣 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗼𝗼𝗹𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮. A server exposes tools and resources, while the agent application acts as the MCP host. It also keeps one client per server. Messages are transferred in the JSON-RPC 2.0 format over stdio for local servers and Streamable HTTP for remote ones.

𝟮. 𝗔𝟮𝗔 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀. With this protocol each agent describes itself by using an Agent Card. This is basically just a JSON file at /.well-known/agent-card.json and contains the agent's skills and how to authenticate. The caller usually sends a task and gets a result. It runs over JSON-RPC, gRPC or HTTP+JSON.

𝟯. 𝗔𝗖𝗣 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘀 𝗮 𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗲 𝗲𝗱𝗶𝘁𝗼𝗿 𝘁𝗼 𝗮 𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁. ACP is the Agent Client Protocol and was created by Zed in 2025. Its authors compare it to LSP, which gave editors one way to talk to every language server. The agent runs as a sub-process of the editor and talks JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio. It also calls back into the editor for permissions, files and the terminal. The editor can also pass its MCP servers to the agent, and the agent then connects to them directly.

Two different protocols have been called ACP. The other one is the Agent Communication Protocol from IBM Research. It was REST-based and agent to agent. 𝗜𝘁 𝗺𝗲𝗿𝗴𝗲𝗱 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗼 𝗔𝟮𝗔 𝗼𝗻 𝟮𝟵 𝗔𝘂𝗴𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟱. So a comparison that shows A2A and ACP as two ways for agents to talk is out of date.

They are also not equally mature. MCP and A2A are both hosted by the Agentic AI Foundation (at the Linux Foundation). The Agent Client Protocol covers coding agents only, and Zed and JetBrains govern it. Its remote transport is still in progress.

In our company we have built an MCP server which enables our customers to use ChatGPT and Claude to do their own reporting, and even to schedule them. This is convenient as we don't need to build every report from scratch.

So, MCP is a good start, because an agent with good tools can cover most of the cases. Use A2A only if you need to connect to another agent. | 11 comments on LinkedIn

𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐢𝐬 𝐧𝐨 𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐥𝐞 “𝐛𝐞𝐬𝐭” 𝐀𝐈 𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐚𝐫𝐜𝐡𝐢𝐭𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞. 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐫𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭 𝐩𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐧 𝐝𝐞𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐬 𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐰.

𝐀𝐬 𝐀𝐈 𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐛𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞, 𝐬𝐢𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐲 𝐚𝐝𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐢𝐬𝐧’𝐭 𝐞𝐧𝐨𝐮𝐠𝐡.

You need to decide how reasoning, execution, coordination, and human control should work together.

Here are the key architecture patterns:

→ ReAct → Think, act, observe, and repeat until the goal is achieved.

→ Planner–Executor → Separate planning from execution for complex, multi-step tasks.

→ Reflection → Generate, evaluate, reflect, and improve the output.

→ Routing → Analyze the request and send it to the most suitable specialized agent.

→ Sequential → Multiple agents work one after another when each step depends on the previous result.

→ Parallel → Multiple agents handle independent sub-tasks simultaneously and their results are combined.

→ Hierarchical → A manager agent delegates tasks to specialized agents and aggregates their results.

→ Human-in-the-loop → Add human approval or review at critical points where safety or accuracy matters.

The interesting part is that these patterns solve different problems.

Need iterative tool use?

→ ReAct

Need structured multi-step planning?

→ Planner–Executor

Need better output quality?

→ Reflection

Have multiple specialized agents?

→ Routing

Have dependent tasks?

→ Sequential

Have independent tasks?

→ Parallel

Need multi-agent coordination?

→ Hierarchical

Need human oversight?

→ Human-in-the-loop

The key takeaway:

Don’t choose an architecture because it looks more advanced. Choose the pattern that matches the workflow.

Save this cheat sheet for your next AI agent project.

🚨 The 4-Layer Architecture Behind AI Agent Systems .

Building an AI Agent isn't just about choosing an LLM.

A production-ready agent system needs multiple layers working together:

1️⃣ LOOP — Observe → Act → Verify → Repeat
The agent observes the environment, executes an action, validates the result, and repeats until the goal is achieved.
→ Observe actual responses
→ Perform controlled actions
→ Verify with tests/evaluations
→ Stop when the goal is reached

2️⃣ GRAPH — Connect Multiple Loops
Graphs determine what happens next based on the current state.
→ Nodes = task units
→ Conditional edges = routing logic
→ Shared state = common data layer
→ Checkpoints = recovery & replay

3️⃣ HARNESS — Connect the LLM to Reality
The runtime layer gives the model access to external systems.
→ Tools
→ Permissions
→ Context
→ Traces
This is where the model gets the capabilities and boundaries required to actually perform work.

4️⃣ META-HARNESS — Manage Multiple Agents
A centralized control layer for multiple agent environments.
→ Agent composition
→ Delegation rules
→ Shared sessions
→ Policies
→ Collaboration
→ Sandboxed environments

The big idea?

Think of an AI Agent system as:
Loop → Graph → Harness → Meta-Harness

The LLM provides the intelligence, but these layers provide the execution, control, coordination, and governance around it.

The future of AI engineering isn't just better models — it's better agent architecture.

author: Prashant U.
post_text:
Python is finally getting explicit lazy imports.

Python 3.15 introduces PEP 810, bringing a language-level mechanism to defer importing modules until they are actually needed.

The idea is simple:

Don't pay the cost of loading a dependency until you use it.

For large Python applications, especially CLI tools, this can make a meaningful difference.

PEP 810 reports:

50–70% faster startup in real-world workloads
30–40% lower memory usage in large applications

The biggest gains come when an application has a large dependency tree but only touches a small portion of it during a particular execution.

And that is increasingly common in modern AI/GenAI applications with dependencies for:

→ LLM providers
→ Vector databases
→ Cloud SDKs
→ Observability
→ Database drivers
→ Optional integrations

One important limitation:

Lazy imports are designed for module scope. They don't replace the traditional technique of importing something inside a function when you specifically need function-level deferral.

Python also provides mechanisms such as "__lazy_modules__" to help adopt lazy imports without necessarily rewriting every import statement.

There is a trade-off.

Import errors and import-time side effects can now be deferred until first use, meaning some failures may surface later than they traditionally would.

So this isn't simply about making every import lazy.

It's about giving Python developers more control over application startup cost.

And there's an interesting timing detail:

Python 3.15 was originally scheduled for October 1, but the final release was postponed after last-minute issues around lazy imports.

New target: October 9, 2026.

Small language feature.

Potentially significant impact for large Python applications.

author: Madan Agrawal
post_text:
Model Context Protocol (MCP) provides a standardized way for AI applications to connect with external tools, data sources, and enterprise systems.

Instead of tightly coupling every AI application with APIs, databases, and business platforms, MCP introduces a common interface between the AI layer and those capabilities.

Its architecture is built around Hosts, Clients, and Servers, with MCP Servers exposing capabilities through Tools, Resources, and Prompts.

Tools allow AI models to invoke operations, while Resources provide readable context that applications can use during reasoning.

MCP does not replace APIs, RAG, or function calling—instead, it can work alongside them and provide a more consistent integration layer.

By centralizing the AI-facing integration layer, MCP can also reduce maintenance overhead, since changes to backend systems can often be handled in the MCP server rather than across multiple AI integrations.

For enterprise AI, this can improve modularity, portability, security boundaries, and the ability to evolve integrations without tightly coupling them to a specific AI application.

author: Omkar Biswal
post_text:
Python 3.15 has a feature that backend developers should pay attention to. ⚡

Lazy Imports.

Normally, when Python sees:

import json
import pandas
import heavy_module

those modules are loaded immediately.

Python 3.15 lets you explicitly defer that work:

lazy import json
lazy import heavy_module

Now the module is loaded only when you actually use it.

Think about a large FastAPI application:

❌ Traditional approach

Application starts
→ Load many dependencies
→ Execute module-level code
→ Initialize unused components
→ Server becomes ready

✅ Lazy imports

Application starts
→ Server becomes ready ⚡
→ Request needs a module
→ Module loads
→ Continue execution

This can be especially interesting for:

• Large Python applications
• CLI tools
• AWS Lambda / serverless workloads
• Applications with large dependency trees
• Reducing unnecessary startup work

But there is a trade-off:

The first use of a lazy import pays the loading cost.

So the goal isn't:

"Make every import lazy."

It's:

"Load expensive dependencies only when they're actually needed."

That's the kind of optimization I find interesting in Python 3.15 — not just new syntax, but changes that can affect how we design production systems.

author: Muhammad Usman Shahbaz
post_text:
RAG isn’t the only way to give LLMs better context.

If you’ve been building AI applications, you’ve probably heard of RAG.

But there’s another approach gaining attention:

CAG — Context-Augmented Generation.

So what’s the difference?

RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)
→ User asks a question
→ Query is converted into a searchable representation
→ Relevant information is retrieved from a knowledge base
→ Retrieved context is added to the prompt
→ LLM generates the answer

RAG is especially useful when your knowledge is large, changing, or difficult to fit into the model context.

CAG (Context-Augmented Generation)
→ Prepare the relevant knowledge in advance
→ Keep it available as context
→ Inject that context when needed

Generate the response from the provided knowledge

CAG can be attractive when the knowledge base is smaller, relatively stable, and fits comfortably within the context window.

The key difference:
RAG → Retrieve what you need.
CAG → Preload what you need.

And this leads to an important architectural decision:

You don't automatically need RAG for every AI application.

If your knowledge is small and stable, loading the relevant context directly can be simpler.

If your knowledge is huge or constantly changing, retrieval becomes much more valuable.

The real skill isn't choosing RAG or CAG.

It's knowing when each architecture makes sense.

Write it once. Reuse it everywhere.
Bash functions turn repetitive commands into clean, powerful automation.

As Bash scripts grow, repeating the same commands can make them harder to read, maintain, and update. Functions solve this by letting you organize tasks into reusable blocks of code.

A function is a block of code designed to perform a specific task. You define it once and call it whenever you need it.

They help you:

🔹 Avoid code repetition
🔹 Keep scripts organized
🔹 Make automation easier to maintain
🔹 Reuse the same logic across tasks

User-Defined Functions: Create your own reusable tasks.

Built-in Functions:
Use Bash commands such as echo, cd, printf, and read.
Functions with Arguments: Pass values to make functions more flexible and reusable.

3. Real-World DevOps Use

Functions can be used to automate common tasks such as:

🔹 Checking whether services are running
🔹 Installing required packages
🔹 Managing servers
🔹 Handling repetitive deployment tasks
🔹 Performing system checks

Instead of writing the same logic again and again, create a function and reuse it whenever needed.

4. Best Practices

For better Bash scripts:

🔹 Use meaningful function names
🔹 Keep functions small and focused
🔹 Use arguments when flexibility is needed
🔹 Add comments for clarity
🔹 Handle errors and edge cases

Why Functions Matter in DevOps

The goal isn't just to write more Bash code.

Automation is not autonomy!

Today we’re launching DBtune 4.0, and from an AI-product perspective, that distinction matters.

Automating a database task is useful, but an autonomous system needs to do more: understand what is happening, determine what needs attention, decide on the right action, act, and learn from the result.

DBtune 4.0 takes an important step in that direction and brings together:

- Server parameter tuning
- Index optimization
- Autovacuum monitoring

This broader approach helps DBtune understand more of what affects #PostgreSQL performance and stability, identify where optimization has the greatest impact, and turn those insights into action through automation, recommendations, and diagnostics.

And autonomy in production has to come with control:

So with DBtune server parameter changes can be automated, or reviewed before they are applied. Index and autovacuum recommendations remain under the user’s control. Guardrails help ensure optimization happens within defined boundaries.

I see the path toward Autonomous PostgreSQL as gradual: Moving from AI advice to AI acting, as confidence, context, and control increase.

DBtune 4.0 is an important step along that path. I’m looking forward to seeing how teams use it in real PostgreSQL environments.

author: Sai Reddy
post_text:
🤖 AI Agents: 5 Architecture Patterns Every AI Architect Should Know

Building an AI Agent is not just about connecting an LLM to a few tools.
The execution pattern you choose determines the system's latency, cost, reliability, scalability, and level of autonomy.

Here are 5 important patterns:

🔹 1. Single-Shot / Direct Invocation
Input → LLM → Output
Best for classification, extraction, summarization, and simple transformations.

🔹 2. Iterative ReAct
Decide → Act → Observe → Repeat
Best for tool-using agents, research, database lookups, and dynamic problem solving.

🔹 3. Planner–Executor
Plan → Decompose → Execute → Aggregate
Useful for complex workflows where tasks can be independently executed and monitored.

🔹 4. Reflexive Agent
Generate → Critique → Refine
Useful when output quality matters and iterative improvement is valuable.

🔹 5. Verifier-Gated Agent
Generate → Verify → Pass/Reject → Execute
Critical for high-risk workflows such as payments, compliance, authorization, and policy enforcement.

🏗️ Production-grade Agent Architecture

These patterns don't have to exist in isolation.

A robust system can combine:
Planner + ReAct Executors + Memory/State + Reflexive Review + Verifier + Guardrails + Observability

The key principle is:
Don't make an agent more autonomous than the problem requires.
Start with the simplest pattern that solves the problem, then introduce planning, iteration, reflection, or verification only when they provide measurable value.

Right pattern → Right use case → Reliable AI system.

author: Raju Dandigam
post_text:
8 RAG architectures explained!

RAG has evolved far beyond a simple vector database + LLM setup.

Depending on the use case, you may need better retrieval, richer context, correction loops, graph relationships, or full agent orchestration.

Here are 8 architectures worth understanding:

→ Naive RAG
The standard flow: query → embedding → vector DB → prompt → LLM.

→ Multimodal RAG
Extends retrieval beyond plain text and supports richer data sources.

→ HyDE
Generates a hypothetical response first, then uses it to improve retrieval.

→ Corrective RAG
Analyzes the query, checks retrieved information, and corrects weak context using search.

→ Graph RAG
Combines vector retrieval with knowledge graphs to capture relationships between entities.

→ Hybrid RAG
Uses vector databases and graph databases together for broader context.

→ Adaptive RAG
Decides whether retrieval is needed and dynamically chooses the right retrieval path.

→ Agentic RAG
Adds memory, planning, an orchestrator, multiple agents, and external tools through MCP servers.

The important part is not choosing the most advanced architecture.

It is choosing the one that matches the problem.

Simple Q&A may only need Naive RAG.
Relationship-heavy systems may benefit from Graph RAG.
Complex enterprise workflows may need Adaptive or Agentic RAG.

Which one are you working with right now? | 65 comments on LinkedIn

author: AI Coach John
post_text:
Your LLM judge can be wrong too.
LLM-as-a-judge makes evaluation scalable, but it comes with its own biases. The trick isn't to blindly trust the judge. It's to evaluate the evaluator.

Here’s the production approach:

1. Choose the right judge
→ Pointwise for monitoring
→ Pairwise for ship/no-ship decisions
→ Reference-based when there is a known answer
→ Rubric-based for long-form evaluation

2. Know the biases
→ Position bias: prefers the first answer
→ Verbosity bias: longer answers score higher
→ Self-preference: favors its own model family
→ Format bias: confident formatting can inflate scores

3. Fix them
→ Swap answer order and vote
→ Use cross-family judges
→ Blind and normalize outputs
→ Use anchored 1–5 rubrics
→ Ask for reasoning before the final verdict

4. Calibrate before trusting it
Use around 200 human-labelled examples and compare judge-human agreement.
Track:
→ Agreement
→ Cohen's κ
→ Confusion matrix
→ Performance by slice
Recalibrate whenever the judge, rubric, or domain changes.

5. Don't judge everything
→ Code → run tests
→ SQL → execute and compare results
→ Math → compute the answer
→ Extraction → exact/F1
→ Safety-critical decisions → human expert

The key lesson:
A judge is still a model.
Calibrate it. Blind it. Swap it. And inspect its worst mistakes.

Save this for your next LLM evaluation pipeline.

author: Anupam Rao
post_text:
Someone in your next AI meeting will say "MCP."
Most of the room will nod and hope nobody asks them to explain it.

MCP stands for Model Context Protocol.
It's an open protocol for connecting AI agents to the tools and data where your work happens.
The official docs compare it to a USB-C port for AI apps.

Without it, every tool needs its own custom integration. Four tools, four separate builds.
With it, the agent talks to MCP, and MCP talks to your tools.

Your existing APIs stay. MCP servers often call them underneath.

Where it sits in an agent setup:
Your agent app runs an MCP client.
The client connects to one or more MCP servers.
Each server offers the tools and data it's been set up to share.

OpenAI's Agents SDK already works with MCP, from servers on your own machine to remote ones the Responses API calls as hosted tools.

Save this for the day your team picks its first agent project.

5 things MCP changes that most AI demos skip over:

1. One connection reaches many tools
↳ Point the agent at an MCP server and it sees a clean list of actions like "create ticket" or "get customer."

2. Integrations become reusable
↳ Build a server once and share it across projects and teams. Adding or swapping a tool later means less rewiring.

3. Servers expose three things
↳ Use tools for actions, resources for data like files or records, and prompts for reusable templates.

4. It runs where you need it
↳ Keep a server local on your own machine over stdio, or host it remotely over HTTP.

5. Trust decides what connects
↳ Connect only servers you trust, because their tools act with the credentials you hand them. Check that access rules hold for private data and write actions before anything goes live.

C# 14 is here. These are the 7 features you need to know:

𝟭. 𝗘𝘅𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗠𝗲𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗿𝘀
You can now define extension properties, static members, and operators, not just methods. Want sequence.IsEmpty instead of sequence.IsEmpty()? Now you can.

This changes how we build C# libraries. Extension methods were always a workaround. This makes them first-class.

𝟮. 𝗟𝗮𝗺𝗯𝗱𝗮 𝗣𝗮𝗿𝗮𝗺𝗲𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗲𝗿𝘀
You can now use ref, out, in, and scoped on lambda parameters without spelling out the type. The compiler infers it from the delegate.

No more writing (string text, out int result) when (text, out result) says the same thing.

𝟯. 𝗡𝘂𝗹𝗹-𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗱𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗔𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁
customer?.Name = value finally works. The right side only evaluates if the left side isn't null.

We've had ?. for reading since C# 6. It took 10 years to get it for writing. Also works with += and -=.

𝟰. 𝗙𝗶𝗲𝗹𝗱 𝗞𝗲𝘆𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗱
Access the compiler-generated backing field directly in your getter or setter using the field keyword. No more declaring private fields for simple validation.

Keep auto-property syntax for the accessor you don't customize. Write only the one you need.

𝟱. 𝗻𝗮𝗺𝗲𝗼𝗳 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗨𝗻𝗯𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱 𝗚𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗰𝘀
nameof(List<>) now returns "List". Previously you had to specify a type argument just to get the name.

Small fix, but useful in source generators and logging where you don't care about the type parameter.

𝟲. 𝗙𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁-𝗖𝗹𝗮𝘀𝘀 𝗦𝗽𝗮𝗻<𝗧>
Implicit conversions between string, T[], Span<T>, and ReadOnlySpan<T>. No more calling .AsSpan() everywhere.

Pass a string directly to a method that takes ReadOnlySpan<char>. The compiler handles it.

author: Mark Varnas
post_text:
We moved a financial client's SQL Server from 2016 to 2025. Up to 4 terabytes.

Same instance size. Lower CPU usage in the period after the move.

In the earlier chart, spikes reached around 40 to 50%. In the later chart, they stayed below 40%.

Useful result. But there's another part of the story I'd want a CTO to hear.

Before the migration, our team ran workload replay for a week. Daniil described a lot of preparation and testing before the move.

That is the reason we do it. Capture the production workload, replay it on the new environment, and compare call by call. You know before cutover whether performance holds, and you know what size the new instance actually needs to be.

Sometimes that is the same number of cores. Sometimes it is half, or a quarter.

This was the second migration we had done for this client, and it went smoothly. One firewall configuration issue to work through.

So the chart is not the end of it. Same instance, lower CPU, means there is now headroom to reduce the instance size. That is where the licensing money is.

This is one client's result. Your workload needs its own comparison.

If you're planning an upgrade, ask what the team will replay, how they'll compare performance, and which connections need checking before the move.

author: Husnain Syed
post_text:
Your C# has never met your CPU.

It compiles to CIL, Common Intermediate Language, not to machine code. In #dotnet the compiler writes CIL and metadata into a .dll, and the CLR, the Common Language Runtime, turns that into machine code while the program runs, one method at a time, on whatever machine it happens to be. I read the IL my own code compiles to. This is what it says.

→ 01. What the compiler produces

A .dll of CIL plus metadata. The file header on mine says Windows, Intel 80386. I ran it on a Mac with an ARM chip and it worked, because nothing inside it is machine code yet.

→ 02. What CIL is

A stack machine. ldarg.0 pushes an argument; ret returns what's on top. There are no registers, and no CPU is named anywhere. Boxing an int is one instruction: box. Unboxing is one too: unbox.any, a type check and a copy together.

→ 03. What the CLR does with it

It loads your types, lays objects out in memory, resolves every method call and frees what nothing references. Then it hands each method to the JIT compiler the first time it's called. On my run that was 8 methods in 3.6 milliseconds, turned into native code for an ARM CPU the compiler never knew about.

→ 04. What the IL shows that the source hides

I passed a struct as its interface, and the box instruction showed up in the caller: five bytes of IL I never wrote. I passed the same struct to a generic constraint and got ldarga.s and a constrained. prefix, with no box at all. That prefix is the entire reason generic constraints are free.

→ 05. How to read it yourself

Sixty lines of C# is all it takes. Reflection gives you the IL bytes of any method, and System.Reflection.Emit.OpCodes names every one. You don't need ildasm, and there's nothing to download.

The principle underneath: the source isn't the program. Everything between them is a translation, and every translation can be read.

author: Rustler
post_text:
Burn 0.22 just shipped. The deep learning framework written in Rust got significantly faster to build, train, and deploy. 🦀

The headline change: backend generics are gone from user-facing code.

Before:
pub struct Model<B: Backend> { linear: Linear<B> }

After:
pub struct Model { linear: Linear }

The backend is now selected through the device, not wired through every type. This breaks the compilation dependency chain that previously propagated through the entire application. Real measured rebuild times:
→ CNN project: 28.42s → 4.57s (6.2x faster)
→ Transformer project: 14.73s → 1.00s (14.7x faster)

That's not a microbenchmark, those are real model-edit rebuilds on release builds.

Training performance on CUDA also improved significantly:
→ CNN: 80% higher throughput, 49% less peak VRAM (956 MiB → 486 MiB)
→ Transformer: 3.6% faster, 18% less VRAM

The VRAM reduction comes from adaptive memory pools that tune allocation sizes based on workload statistics, no manual configuration needed.

What else is in 0.22:

LoRA and QLoRA fine-tuning : attach low-rank adapters to frozen base weights, with per-parameter-group optimizer config. QLoRA keeps base weights quantized to reduce storage.

ONNX export : export a Burn model to ONNX with one call. Early stage, limited operator coverage, but the direction is there.

Remote compute via Iroh : run inference and training on another machine's GPU. Peer-to-peer, encrypted, authenticated. Repeated graph sequences are sent once and replayed by ID.

CubeCL Environment : ship pre-warmed compilation and autotuning caches with your application. Works across native, WASM, and no_std targets.

Graph capture and replay on CUDA and HIP : reuse kernel launch sequences without repeating launch preparation.

NDArray and LibTorch backends are deprecated. Candle is removed. Requires Rust 1.95+.

The team also hints at a native AI engine (LLM inference server + chat app + OpenAI-compatible API, all in Rust) shipping soon on top of Burn. Worth watching.

author: Danial Amin
post_text:
If you are using an LLM to evaluate another LLM, there are a few questions worth asking first:
Do different LLM judges agree?
Does that agreement hold when the context or level of risk changes?
Can the judge give a short justification that actually supports its score?
And is the judge independent of the model that generated the output?
These questions are at the center of our new paper with Joni Salminen, and Bernard Jim Jansen, now published in Technological Forecasting and Social Change (IF: 13.5; CiteScore: 30.5).
We tested GPT-4o, Claude 3 Sonnet, and Gemini 1.5 Pro as judges of AI-generated personas.
A few key results:
• Agreement was moderate overall, but varied across generators and contexts.
• Individual-level agreement declined from ICC = .55 in peer tutoring to .34 in mandatory training.
• Non-compliance with the required justification increased to 34–49% for persona-set evaluation.
• The study also raises the circularity problem when the same model families appear on both the generation and evaluation sides.
For me, this suggests a practical evaluation procedure:
1. ask each judge for a score and a short justification, 2. check whether the justification follows the rubric, 3. compare judgments across multiple models, 4. examine whether agreement changes across contexts or risk levels, and 5. calibrate against humans where appropriate.
This also aligns closely with Anthropic's recent guidance for rigorous evaluations, particularly around validating graders, manually inspecting evaluation outputs, reporting inter-rater agreement, testing across severity levels, and avoiding circular AI-as-judge setups.

post_text:
MCP is quickly becoming the bridge between AI assistants and enterprise data.

The real question is whether that bridge is governed.

• MCP can standardize how AI tools connect to files, applications, and business systems

• Enterprise deployments need per operation authorization, secure credential handling, audit logging, scope controls, and rate limiting

• A governed MCP layer can extend existing security and compliance policies to AI without creating a separate governance stack

author: Pamela Fox
post_text:
I had a great time at PyBay this weekend! Besides giving my own talk on vector embeddings, I got to see some excellent talks from the community:

✅ "Is TDD even relevant anymore? Yes, but don't be dumb about it." by Brian Okken
Brian introduced "Lean TDD", which borrows from several TDD styles: test against the API, test behavior rather than implementation, and start from acceptance criteria. He also showed his version of the "testing trophy": a few UI tests, mostly API tests, not too many unit tests, and static analysis at the base. Learn more at https://leantdd.com. Brian also wrote "Python Testing with pytest", which I highly recommend!

🗄️ "Talk Python in Production" by Michael Kennedy
Michael showed how he runs all of Talk Python on a simple setup that he manages himself. I loved his tips for reducing memory use:
• Use async web frameworks so each worker can handle more requests
• Move memory-heavy work into subprocesses
• Use raw queries instead of an ORM. It uses much less memory, and coding agents are good at writing SQL (but make sure to parameterize!)
• Use lazy imports, which are built into Python 3.15
• Move in-memory caches to SQLite with diskcache

🧵 "Getting Started with Free-Threaded Python Using NumPy" by Christopher Ariza
Christopher argued that free-threading "may be the greatest enhancement to Python performance." His final tip was to "talk to your agents about concurrency." Agents tend to write serial code first, so review their code and ask for concurrency. They can also quickly benchmark the alternatives for you.

🦀 "The Path to Introducing Rust in CPython" by Emma Smith
Emma explained the dangers of undefined behavior in C and how Rust prevents memory errors and data races by default. New Python extensions are now choosing Rust more often than C. The roadmap aims for an optional Rust build with zlib in Rust in Python 3.16 (Oct 2027), then more modules like io and json after that. More at https://lnkd.in/gu4XTC34

🧠 "How Contexts Fail (and How to Fix Them)" by Drew Breunig
Drew described how our focus has moved from prompt engineering to context engineering to harness engineering. He covered four ways contexts fail: poisoning, distraction, confusion, and "fighting the weights." Even long-context models get distracted past roughly 100–200k tokens. He showed how to add compaction with DSPy, using a small model to label each chunk of context as hide, summarize, or show.

🧪 "Testing the Nondeterministic: Making Safe Changes in your Agent Harness" by Felipe Perez Chichasov
Felipe shared how his team built evals in code for an internal agent, using a custom evals framework they wrote themselves.

Thanks to the PyBay organizers and volunteers for another great conference! See you at PyBay 2027 on October 23! 🐍

author: Andrii Nikishaiev UA
post_text:
Most Postgres databases have indexes that nobody uses.

They take disk space. They slow down every insert and update. And they stay for years, because nobody checks.

Postgres already tracks this for you. Two system views show most of what you need:
- pg_stat_user_indexes: how often each index is used (idx_scan)
- pg_stat_user_tables: dead rows, autovacuum, HOT updates

A few quick rules I use:
- idx_scan = 0 and not unique? It’s a candidate to drop.
- Unique or primary key? Always keep it.
- An index on (a) and another on (a, b)? The first one isn’t needed.
- Low HOT update rate? Too many indexes on columns that change often.

Two traps to check before you drop anything:

- When were the stats last reset?
- Did you check the replicas? Their reads don’t show up on the primary.

And always use DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY.

author: Konstantin Beregovoy
post_text:
You use the standard TypeScript types. That is a good default.

But there is another option.

modern-web-types, from Philip Walton, is a package of type definitions that replaces or extends lib.dom.d.ts. It is not a library with functions.

How it differs from the standard types
Official TypeScript types are conservative. They include only APIs implemented in at least two browser engines. This protects you from accidentally using something that works in one browser only.

Walton's package lowers the threshold to one engine. That brings types for the View Transition API, the Long Animation Frame API, and fetchLater(). The generator is the same as for the official types. Only the input criteria differ.

At the time of the article, the scale is 433 interfaces, 223 global variables, and 311 new properties and methods.

The package stays current
This is not a manual project. Once a week an automated job runs the generator on fresh data and compares the result with the last published version. If something changed, a PR is opened, and after approval a new version is released. So the numbers above are a snapshot, not a constant.

But it is not an upgrade
Here is what matters. It is a tradeoff, not a "newer and better version for everyone". For production code that must work for all users, the standard types are safer. TypeScript warns you when an API is not supported everywhere.

Where the package is actually useful
In prototypes and experiments. And where you already knowingly use APIs that exist in only one browser. For example, the View Transition API for page transitions or fetchLater() for analytics when the user leaves the page. In those places you are tired of as any and ignoring type errors.

My take as a Frontend Lead
It is a tool for a specific job, not a default for every project. If you work at the edge of the web platform, give it a try. If you write code for all users, stay on the standard types.

author: Christine Vallaure de la Paz
post_text:
Figma fully covers 45% of CSS and 17% of a component API. The rest is where an agent working on a design system starts to guess, and I've slowly stopped seeing that as a problem. Here is why:

I tallied all 323 items, 204 CSS features and 119 component capabilities, judged against Figma Design this month. The full lists are in the images, and I fed those images into my own system (you're welcome to do the same).

(And before anyone asks why I still use Figma: I think better on a canvas than in a code file, you do you.)

These days I generate from code → Figma and use Figma as a facade, as I've started calling it. Code holds the truth, and the canvas is where I look at it, compose with it and decide whether it's any good. I call this in-system design, designing wherever I want as long as everything points back to code, and there is a lot more to say about it, so more on that soon.

So the red items are the questions the file can't answer. That's fine as long as you know which ones they are, because the answer is already in code and you can point people there. It only goes wrong when nobody knows, and a developer, a designer or an agent fills the gap with a guess.

What I use the list for:
→ Ending the "why can't Figma just do that" chat.
→ Onboarding designers, so they know what to stop looking for in the file and where to find it instead
→ Knowing when to point at code rather than the file, in a handoff or a review
→ Agent context, as a gaps.md it reads before it touches a setup. This is the use I find most interesting, and I'm testing other ways to do it, because a markdown file is something the agent reads, not something it has to obey, so I'm looking into pushing this further.

Why I don't think Figma should to close every gap on the canvas
I'm a big fan of designers having code literacy; it's most of what I teach. But put all of it on the canvas, and Figma becomes a bad code editor, where every design decision needs engineering judgment. For code, use code; for exploration, use the canvas and stay in-system.

Few more things:
- Yes, I still add a contract here
- The numbers undersell one category, mapping and intent, where both sides have a property and quietly mean different things.
- I also only measured against the web here, and most teams also ship iOS and Android, so the same Figma property gets read three times by three platforms, each with its own idea of what it means...so where to point then? I haven't worked that one out yet. I've been reading into Nathan Curtis's work on component specs as structured data, one description of a component that every platform can read from, and I find it really inspiring because it goes straight at this problem for teams like that. Currently playing with his SPECS plugin, very cool stuff, check it out!

How this all started is a longer story, so it gets its own post and an article.
!! If you spot something wrong in the lists, tell me and I'll fix it !!

author: Dr Emmanuel Ogungbemi
post_text:
Don't tell me your LLM is performing well if you haven't looked past accuracy.

A model can score 90% on your benchmark and still embarrass you in production.

Here's why.

LLM evaluation has at least four layers, and skipping any one of them gives you a false picture:

1. Task accuracy, does the model get the right answer on your labelled test set? This is the one everyone measures. It's also the easiest to game.
2. Calibration, when the model says it's confident, is it actually right more often? A confidently wrong LLM is a liability, not an asset.
3. Behavioural consistency, does it give the same answer to semantically identical questions phrased differently? If not, you don't have a reliable system, you have a lucky one.
4. Failure mode distribution, where does it fail, and how badly? Silent hallucinations in low-frequency inputs are harder to catch than obvious errors, and they're the ones that reach your users.

The real trap is treating evaluation as a one-time gate before deployment.

author: Matteo Collina
post_text:
"Do you still read code written by AI?"

That's the question I'm being asked whenever I meet a colleague. It gets to the heart of where our industry is right now.

Here's my honest answer: I use AI every single day. It has made me more productive than I've ever been. I ship fixes to Node.js, Pino, Fastify, and undici constantly, and AI handles much of the implementation.

But I still review every single line that ships.

My bottleneck is no longer how fast I can code. It's how good I am at reviewing. When AI produces a security fix, I don't just check whether the tests pass. I'm asking whether it actually closes the attack vector, fits the architecture, maintains backward compatibility, and is something I can stand behind.

This is the argument I laid out in my newsletter piece "[The Human in the Loop](". I've reviewed and assessed code written by others in open source for over a decade. AI is just another contributor now. I review its PRs the same way I review anyone else's, and I decide if it's good enough.

The moment I stop reviewing is the moment I stop being responsible for what I ship.

I've also been tracking this shift through an academic lens. A paper on the economics of judgment confirmed what I've been arguing from the trenches: the bottleneck has shifted from coding to judgment, and judgment is getting more valuable.

My real worry isn't that software development is dying. It's that we'll build a culture where "I didn't review it, the AI wrote it" becomes an acceptable excuse. When you can generate code at AI speed, the scale of damage from shipping code you don't understand is much larger than it was when you were limited by typing speed.

So do I still read code written by AI? Every single line. The human in the loop isn't a limitation to be optimized away: it's the point. It's what separates shipping something from standing behind it.

author: Sajeev KR
post_text:
Spring Boot Mistakes That Cause Production Problems

Answer is shared in this link - https://lnkd.in/g-TDNtCk

1. Using default database connection pool settings without considering production traffic.

2. Returning JPA entities directly from REST APIs instead of using DTOs.

3. Ignoring the N+1 query problem in Spring Data JPA.

4. Using @Transactional without understanding transaction boundaries and proxy behavior.

5. Calling a @Transactional method from another method in the same class and expecting the transaction to apply.

6. Using unlimited retries when a downstream service is unavailable.

7. Calling external services without connection and read timeouts.

8. Creating large thread pools without understanding the workload and resource limits.

9. Using parallelStream() blindly for production workloads.

10. Loading large datasets into memory instead of using pagination or streaming.

11. Using @Async without properly configuring and monitoring the executor.

12. Storing secrets such as passwords and API keys directly in application.properties.

13. Using the same configuration for development and production.

14. Relying only on logs without metrics, health checks, and distributed tracing.

15. Exposing sensitive information through exception messages or API responses.

16. Using overly broad exception handling such as catch (Exception e) everywhere.

17. Ignoring graceful shutdown during deployments.

18. Running scheduled jobs on every application instance without preventing duplicate execution.

19. Adding caching without planning cache invalidation and stale data handling.

20. Deploying database schema changes that are incompatible with the currently running application version.

21. Using synchronous calls for every microservice interaction when asynchronous processing would be more appropriate.

22. Ignoring idempotency for APIs that perform payments, orders, or other critical operations.

23. Setting Kubernetes CPU and memory limits without understanding the JVM's resource requirements.

24. Using health checks that only verify whether the application process is running instead of checking critical dependencies appropriately.

25. Optimizing code before measuring the actual production bottleneck.

Which Spring Boot mistake have you seen cause the biggest production problem?

author: Steve Barth
post_text:
Burger King changed their bun.
ㅤ
It cost them more, but you can taste the difference.
ㅤ
This summer, McDonald's posted U.S. same-store sales growth of less than one percent…while Burger King's U.S. comparable same-store sales rose eight and a half percent. To me, there is a reason why these two very similar kinds of businesses are diverging at the moment. There are structural shifts at play.
ㅤ
Burger King has experienced the same cost pressures as the rest of the industry, but instead of relying only on price, it invested back into the product and restaurant experience. They changed the bun. They used better ingredients. They set out to hire sixty thousand people to improve the experience at the restaurant.
ㅤ
They invested in what I call productive friction, the kind that costs more, but produces something worthwhile that customers can feel.
ㅤ
Until very recently, McDonald's generally went the other direction: more value meals, lower prices, faster throughput. Everything optimized for volume.
ㅤ
Consumers do not value friction itself. They value what that productive friction prevents you from optimizing away.
ㅤ
These individual decisions by companies can make sense at the time. But eventually the customer feels the accumulated effect. The sandwich is a little worse. The restaurant feels a little more transactional. The product feels more engineered around cost and throughput. Nothing catastrophic happened. You simply optimized away some of the reasons the customer wanted it in the first place.
ㅤ
There are rewards for not optimizing away productive friction across the industry. Cava, for example, is growing same-store sales and traffic at a rapid rate, while Chipotle has returned to positive transaction growth. The brands doing well right now are the ones where quality is the focus, or the willingness to be slower and more deliberate is visible in the product.
ㅤ
In different forms, people keep gravitating toward things that are stubbornly, deliberately human. The places where someone cared about what they were making, at some step along the way.
ㅤ
When you optimize for efficiency at the expense of everything else, quality is the first thing to go. It’s no surprise that people take note.
ㅤ
Think about what that might mean in your organization while you’re picking up lunch today. | 21 comments on LinkedIn

author: Ivan Lungu
post_text:
Node.js just changed how it ships, and it starts this month.

For years, the rule was simple:

Even versions = LTS.
Odd versions = short-lived.

That rule is gone.

Starting with Node 27:
- One major release per year, in April
- Every major release eventually becomes LTS
- 6 months Alpha - 6 months Current - 30 months LTS

What this means for your team:

• Node 26 is the last release under the old model. It enters LTS this month and reaches EOL in April 2029.
• Node 27 enters Alpha this month, becomes Current in April 2027, and reaches LTS in October 2027.
• Still on Node 22? Its EOL is April 2027. Time to start planning the upgrade.

And if you move to Node 26, you also get the Temporal API enabled by default.

Finally, a modern alternative to Date.

The reasoning makes sense: fewer release lines mean less maintenance for a project largely supported by volunteers, while giving teams a more predictable upgrade cycle.

Fewer releases. Less confusion. Longer support.

Honestly, this feels like a change Node.js teams have been waiting for.

author: Usman Abbas
post_text:
A slow API response can overwrite a newer one.

Heres the bug:

A user types "re", then "react".
→ Request A ("re") is slow
→ Request B ("react") is fast
→ B arrives first, so the UI shows "react" results
→ Then A arrives and overwrites them with "re" results

No error. No crash. Just wrong data on screen.

The cause: requests dont always finish in the order they started.

How to prevent it:
🔹 AbortController
Cancel the previous request when the input changes. In a useEffect, return () => controller.abort() from the cleanup, and ignore the AbortError so it doesnt show up as a real failure.

🔹 Ignore flag or request ID
Set a flag in the effect cleanup, or compare each response against the latest request ID, and drop anything stale. This is the pattern in Reacts own docs.

🔹 Use a data-fetching library
TanStack Query and SWR tie results to the query key, so a late response for an old key cant replace the current one.

Two things to remember:
- Debouncing reduces requests, but it doesnt remove the race.
- Aborting stops the browser request, but your server may still finish the work, so keep writes idempotent.

Do you cancel requests in your effects, or rely on a library?

author: DFIR Lab
post_text: Nest is a framework for building scalable Node.js server-side applications. Versions prior to 11.1.11 have a Fastify URL encoding middleware bypass. A NestJS application is vulnerable if it uses `@nestjs/platform-fastify`; relies on `NestMiddleware` (via `MiddlewareConsumer`) for security checks (authentication, authorization, etc.), or through `app.use()`; and applies middleware to specific routes using string paths or controllers (e.g., `.forRoutes('admin')`). Exploitation can result in unauthenticated users accessing protected routes, restricted administrative endpoints becoming accessible to lower-privileged users, and/or middleware performing sanitization or validation being skipped. This issue is patched in `@nestjs/platform-fastify@11.1.11`.
